A cooErNia CLUB—The rolling-pin. A CONSCIENTIOUS milkman never wears pumps. NOTE THIS !—An auctioneer does as he is bid, 5 postman as he is directed. WHEN a cat gives an entertainment from the top of a wall, it isn't the cat we object to, it's the waul. "WHAT is the worst thing about riches?" asked the Sunda) _;hool teacher; and the new boy said —" Not having any." " MA, if you give me an apple, I will be good.* "No, my child, you must not be good for pay— you ought to be good for nothing." A WAG, seeing a door nearly off its hinges, in whiCh condition it had been some time, observed that when it had fallen and killed some one it would probably be hung. JoHNyr is just beginning to learn geography. He says that the Poles live partly at one end of the globe and partly at the other. He knows that it is so, because it is marked on the map. A BAD little boy rubbed cayenne pepper well over the back of his jacket. The schoolmaster thrashed him briskly,', but dismissed school im- mediately, to run to the nearest chemist for eye- water. "PA, what does a wooden wedding mean?" Pa, looking over his paper—" It means, ray son, that if the wedded parties were free, they 'wooden' get married agAin. That's all." SOCRATES, when a chatterbox applied to him to be taught rhetoric, said "that he must pay double the usual fee, because it would first be necessary to teach him to hold his tongue." IMPASSIONED LOVER, quoting Moore, in a whis- per, "Our couch shall be roses, bespangled with dew.* Practical Girl—" It would give me rheu- matics, and so it would you."

THERE Is a policeman named Moon. Quite ap- propriately he is on the night force; and like the other one, he is about half the time invisible. "Do you believe in luck, my good man 7 " asked a superstitious old lady of a tramp. "I can't say that I do, mum," replied the tramp, "because I've never had any."

"I SAY, Jenkins, can you tell a young, tender chicken from an old, tough one ? " "Of course I can." "Well, how 7" "By the teeth." "Chickens have no teeth." "No, but I have." A CONUNDRUM FOR THE TIMID.—Why should people never be frightened at the appearance of a ghost ? Because, if it is a ghost, its appearance must, in the nature of things, be immaterial.

A saoultAKEß with one eye complained that one of his lamps did. not burn. One of his shopmates, who is a genuine son of the Emerald Isle, with astonishment exclaimed: "Faith, and what do you want with two lamps? Ye haven't but one eye!"
"WHAT nonsense 1" exclaimed Bertha. "The

idea of telling Mrs. Brown that you were only twenty-three !" "But didn't I do right, dear ? " replied Edith. "You know mamma has always taught us not to exaggerate. It is better to under- state rather than overstate, you know." WHAT A MARRIED MAN IS LIKE.—A shrewd old lady cautioned her married daughter against worry- ing her husband too much, and conauded by say- ing: "My child, a man is like an egg. Kept in hot water a little while, he may boil soft; but keep him there too long, and he hardens." A COUPLE OP IRISH Birm.s.—Speaking on the much-vexed Irish land-question, a speaker said: ' " The country is overrun by absentee landlords; and, after a magnificent peroration, he said : "I tell you the cup of old Ireland's misery is overflow- ing—ay, and it's not full yet !" THERE are some persons who cannot take a joke, but Suiggins is not one of them. A "friend" acquainted with Sniggin's frequent changes of abode, asked him which he thought was the cheaper —to move or pay rent. "I can't tell you, my dear boy," replied Sniggins ; "I have always moved." "I SAT, Johnny," whispered Augustus Longreach, " was your sister pleased to learn that I had called upon her ? " " You bet she was," answered Johnny. " When ma told her that you'd, called while she was 'out, she clasped her hands and said, Thank Heaven!' and.she meant it too," added Johnny.

EL WIDOW in Japan who is willing to think of matrimony, wears her hair tied and twisted around a long shell hair-pin placed horizontally across the back of the head. "Were this the custom in this country," writes a waggish editor, "we should throw down the pen, and at once engage in the manufacture of long shell hair-pins." lc CHILD NOT WANTING IN OBSERVATION.—A school-board inspector asked the members of a girls' sewing-class the other day: "Who can tell me what basting a turkey means?" There was silence for a while, and then a little miss signified that she knew. "Well, what is it T' said the inspector. "Sewing up the place where the stuffin' goes in," was the reply. aIIORGLE FELT HE WAS SAFE.—They were stand- ing at the front gate. "Won't you come into the parlour and sit a little while, Georgie, dear?" "N -o; I tisink not." replied George, hesitatingly. "I wish yon would," the girl went on; "it's awfully lone- some. Mother has gone out, and father is upstairs grooming with rheumatism in the feet." "Both feet 1" asked George. "Yes, both feet." Then ru come in."

13 BOYLZ ROCITE was, in his day, the droll of the House of Commons, and was continually per-
pedaling bulls, which Curran used to insist Were the result of preparation. Hi i celebrated one, con-

f mulcting age plst and present, deserves a record. "Mg. Speaker," said he, I don't see why we should put ourselves out a the way to benefit posterity. What has posterity ever done for us 7" When the roar which followed had subsided, Sir Boyle entered upon a lucid explanation. "By posterity, sir, I do not mean our ancestors, but those who were to come immediately after them."

.down to Oxford and caused same fun. He- called
for subjects, and amongst the half-dozen that pre- taented themselves was one young gentleman who had far more sense of humour than discretion.

Imagined. RIB T. ROBINSON was a tall, uncouth man, and his stature was often rendered still more remarkable by his hunting dress, a postilion's cap, a tight green jacket, and buckskin breeches. He was liable to sudden whims, and once set off on a sudden in his hunting suit, to visit his sister, who was married and settled at Paris. He arrived while there was a large company at dinner. The servant announced M. .Robinson, and he came in, to the great amazement of the guests. Among others a French ablyS thrice lifted his fork to his mouth, and thrice laid it down,
with an eager stare of surprise. Unable. to restrain
his curiositY any longer, he burst out with, "Pardon- nez moi, naonsieur, est-ce que vous ites le celebre Robinson Crusoe 1"
THE exclamation of the Irish legislator,. "Hark!

I smell a rat; but I will nip it in the bud," is usually quoted as the most striking example of what Mrs. Malaprop would call a "derangement" of metaphors. But in the correspondence column of the Bridge- water Mercury there is a somewhat similar instance of metaphorical confusion. A certain Mr. F. 0. Temblett, in the course of delivering his soul on the question of Fair Trade, mentions Mr. Howard Vincent's conversion to Toryism, and his subsequent heresy on.the subject of Protection. "I shall not find fault with him for • his change of politics," " brit I do find fault with him for attempting to trail a red herring across the Conservative path, which may, if not nipped in the bud, lead to an Infinity of mischief.' COMING out of church the other morning, a lady whispered to her friend, "I couldn't possibly give anything to the collection, my dear, for my money had got so hopelessly mixed up with my lozenges."

"CAPITAL CHAT."
The decision as to the custody of the children in the O'Shea case puts £2,000 a year at the dis- posal of Captain O'Shea.

~.Parliament will be opened by Royal Commission at 2 p.m. on Tuesday next. The House of Lords will afterwards meet at 4.15 p.m., when the Address will be moved by Lord Windsor and seconded by Lord Ardilaun.

General Master Workman Powderly, of the American Knights of Labor, has issued a ballot ask- ing all members of the order whether they favor the formation of an independent political party. Up to now, labor has had a very insignificant influence in American politics.

A Helsingfors Correspondent writes: A sad in- cident has just occurred here. The dead body of a young man has been found in the Borga Cemetery. His wife died a fortnight ago, and this brought him so low that his friends were afraid he would never get over it. He had at last taken a pillow, gone to his wife's grave, and laid himself down and died.

Dr. Lyman Abbott (Beecher's successor), who has just made an extended trip through England, expresses this interesting judgment about the Anglican Church :—" Sententiously expressed, the Established Church of England of to-day appears to me to be a beautiful momument to the life of the past, rather than a skilfully adapted instrument for the work of the future."

A curious hunting incident occurred at High- worth, Wilts, on Saturday afternoon. The N.W.11. hounds stated on the scent of a fox, an&after 25 minutes' run were close upon it, when the animal jumped through an open window—about five feet from the ground—into a school-room. The hounds followed through the window, and caught the fox, which was nearly killed when the huntsman had effected an entrance.

It is understood that an arrangement has been made that Mr. Parnell who will, as soon as the decree for divorce is made absolute, marry Mrs. O'Shea. This, of course, has considerable bearing on Mr. Parnell's position. It does not condone his conduct, but it shows his anxiety to do justice to the woman he has wronged. When his marriage takes place, it will do much to remove the painful impression created by the proceedings in the Divorce Court.

I understand that Mr. Parnell is in better health than he has been for some time past. He intends to take an active part in the business of the coming session.. Between the Special Commission and the divorce case the pressure on his mind for two years past has been extreme, and has to some extent dis- abled him from public work. Both these matters are now ended, and the hon. gentleman intends to throw himself keenly into political work.

"Truth " hears that the relations between the Emperor William and his mother have subsided from bitter hostility into what Lord Beaconfield wculd have defined as "a sort of bad tempered understanding." The Emperor has a morbid jealousy of his mother, and he has made it perfectly plain that he will not permit her to take a leading part even at the Court, and, if his wife cannot fill her proper place at State functions, he will be both Emperor and Empress himself.

According to a letter from a correspondent, the Great Western Company is going to introduce lava- tory accommodation into third-class carriages. This is a much needed concession to the most profitable class of passengers. It is about time that railway companies treated the travelling public with some degree of fairness. If the Great Western introduce lavatories and better accommodation into all its third-class carriages, it will be to its own profit as well as to the comfort of the passengers.

The accounts of the Queen's health, though satis- factory, still dwell on the fact that she is not so active as last year. Every year, in fact, she does less and is more fatigued; and it is said by those about the Court that, though in all essentials she is strong, she feels and acknowledges regretfully this diminution of energy. Her Majesty has fortunately avoided taking cold recently, and this is in her favour, for she is now unable to take any walking exercise, and Is more apt to get chilled when driv- ing.

Miss Martin-Leake, whose appointment to the Secretaryship of the Women's Liberal Federation has just been announced, was a Goldsmith's Scholar at Girton College, whence she graduated three years ago with mathematical honours. To undertake the secretaryship of the Women's Liberal Federation, Miss Martin-Leake resigns the position she now occupies of Assistant Director of Pupil Teachers' Training Classes for the Birmingham School Board, a post to which she had the distinction of being the first woman appointed. She has shown a marked aptitude for organisation and administiatiTe work.

The latest application of electricity to the uses of daily life has been invented and perfected by a New York physician. He has completed telephonic connections between the wards of the City Hospital and the reception-rooms, so that patients suffering from infectious maladies may. safely communicate with their visitors. A board in the reception-room contains the names of the patients, and an attend- ant has only to put the plug into the hole beneath any name when any friend desires to speak with the occupant of a cot upstairs. This has been found to work with great success, and the plan is to be adopted by the other hospitals.

Mr. Harry Quilter has along indictment of-Stan- I ley "as leader and comrade " in this month's " Universal Review." He shows bow inconsistent , Stanley has been in his statements about the rear column, and attempts to clear the character of Major Barttelot. Mr. Quilter has not, however, got at the secret history of the expedition, but collects certain facts which indicate what appears more and more to have been its real character—a plan to grab territory and to " collar " Emits Pasha for the sake of ivory. The promoters, in their capacity of busi- ness men, had heard that Emin had seventy-five tons of ivory, worth £lOO,OOO, and they resolved as philantrophists, to relieve him—of his ivory.

Everybody feels sorry for Sir Walter Barttelot in the calamity which has befallen him. Hc is the last man in the world to deserve it. No kinder-hearted soul ever breathed than the genial old Tory, with his simple, honest face, blunt, outspoken ways, and bowed shoulders. •He is a universal favourite in the House and the Lobby, and he numbers Tories, Whigs, Radicals, and Irishmen among his friends. It is all very tragic—very pitiful.

One of the most significant victories during the American elections was the return of Mr. John de Witt Warner, cbairman of the Tariff Reform Organization, to whose active system of propaganda is due, to a very large extent, the overthrow of Protection. A systematic campaign has been carried on for several years by the Tariff Reform Club, by means of timely pamphlets, investigations, and public meetings. Mr. Warner conducted this work. He was strongly opposed by the Protection- ist manufacturers in the division of New York, for which he stood, but was elected by the enormous majority of 7,333 votes. Mr. Warner is a real tree trader, and is, we behove, the first one returned to the American Congress. Mr. Warner is a young working lawyer. He gives a very large amount of his time to the advocacy of tariff reform, and is one of the leading authorities on the question in America.

Toole is as inveterate a joker as ever. On his way to IN ew Zealand his steamer made a brief stay at Hobart, the capital of Tasmania. He went ashore and made straight for the Theatre Royal, having previously made himself up as an itinerant show- man. Getting an interview with the manager of the Royal, he guilessly7 asked the use of the theatre "for a hacrobatic show. Me and my pardner you see, does big tricks—heavy-weight business, ground and lofty tumbling, hastonishing feats of strength, et cetera." The manager said he was very sorry, but they had come to the wrong shop, and sarcastically suggested that they had better engage the Exhibition building for their entertainment. Toole and his companion then backed out with pro- fuse thanks for the suggestion, and saying he would go there. Afterwards Johnny changed his costume and revealed his identity, whereupon the manager and himself laughed heartily over the joke and the champagne.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 22. 1890.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 22. 1890.
MEETING OF RAILWAY SERVANTS. SHORTER HOURS MOVEMENT.

In connection with the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants, a meeting was held in the League Hall, Warrington, on Sunday evening, when the objects of the Society were fully explained. The attendance, over which Mr. G. Greaves (Warring- ton) presided, was moderate. After a fe ff introductory remarks by the CHAIR- MAN, . .

, Mr. W. HART, of Wigan moved :—" That this meeting condemns the excessive hours of labour that prevail upon our railways, and hails with satisfaction the hours pro- gramme of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Ser- vants, and pledges itself to support the same by all legal means." After commenting on the excessive hours 1. which men on the railway work, Mr. Hart said the short I hours programme was formed at the congress of railway men, held in 1889, in order that they should be relieved, to some extent, of the long hours; and he thought that ten hours per day was quite sufficient, and that was all they were seeking. Other trades had their respective organisations and unions, and it was essential that rail- way men should have an organisation in order to bring about a better feeling amongst themselves, and to make known to the companies that the servants were unani- mous in asking for a reduction of hours of labour. Comm bination was necessary to effect what they desired, for if a memorial was sent to the heads of the various com- panies, from two or three thousand men in their employ they would not take the same notice of it as if it was forwarded by the thirty to fifty thousand men engaged on the systems. He thought it was time that railway employes looked to their own interests, and he was sure that by working long hours they were not doing so. They had it on medical authority that eight hours labour a day took as much strength , as could be replaced by eight hours sleep and eight hours recreation, so that railway men, who were working 14, 15, and 16 hours a day were ruining their constitution. (Shame.) Again, the same medical authority said that the workers died, on the average, at 29 years, and that the average age at death of the leizured lot was 56 years. Here, then, was a difference of 27 years, or, literally speaking, the workers died 27 years before their time, simply on account of being overworked. The men who were employed on the railways worked longer hours than most other men, and the only way in which they could ameliorate their condition was by combination, ' and they would have to be dotermined to help one an- other to obtain their just rights. The railway companies, of course, would contend that they could not afford to , grant the concessions sought ; but he (the speaker) , averred that they could well afford to grant them. In the Board of Trade returns they found that the income of the railway companies last year was something like £77,000,000; and their expenditure was .1244,000,000 and that the workers, at the outside, only received £20,000,000. He had recently received a book which L advocated an eight hours day for railway employes, which, all round, the companies could well afford, and if ; this was brought about, it was computed that employ- ment would be found for 170,000 more men, who would receive, on the average, 19s. 3d. per week. This how- ever, they did not ask, and, in conclusion, he urged the , railway workers in Warrington to do their utmost to ) promote the short hours programme. (Applause.) Mr. MCKENNA, of Garston, seconded the resolution and

Mr. PETERS, of Edge Hill, in supporting the same, said an eight hours day was advocated at the Trades Union Congress at Liverpool, and they could depend upon it the day was coming when they would have it. It was not right to let one half of the nation live in luxury, whilst the other half was starving. (Hear, hear.) He had no doubt that a number of petty officials, directors, superintendents, and station-masters, in and around Warrington would t(11 them they were well situated. To this he replied that it was a disgrace to civilised England that they could find men at the present time working 17 and 18 hours a day. He thought no living man could stand in a signal box or on the foot plates from 12 to 14 hours a day without closing his eyes. He (the speaker) had had experience on railways, and he had slept many miles, so exhausted had been his condition. He was pre- , sent to ask them to combine, whatever their occupations , on the line may be, tor the emancipation of labour. They did not want strikes, and personally, he was bitterly opposed to them ; but, he believed this, when they had tried all legitimate and pacific means, their only weapon left was the withholding of labour. (Applause.) What was capital and labour ? They all knew that capital could not exist without labour. If they looked around Warrington in a few years, they would find mansions being erected, and where would the money with which these places would be built come from ? Why, it would be sweated out of the workers. They were the producers of wealth, and, as such, they had a right to expect a fair proportion of it. (Applause.) f they scrutinized the books of the various sick societies, , they would find the effect of men working excessive ' hours ; if they went to the cemetery gates they would find it. If they went to thc several hospitals, they also would find written over it in large letters "through ex- cessive work." He admitted they had good officials in the service ; but it was also a fact that they had bad ones, and the reason they had the latter was attributable solely to the apathy of the workers themselves. , He implored them to put this apathy at one I side, and help forward the object they had in 1 view. Let them sink their nationality, and political differences, and say to one another, "What are your troubles are my troubles." (Applause.) Mr. Peters went on to describe the benefits which accrued to members of the Amalgamated Society, and invited all to join it, for it was to their advantage to do so, and con- cluded by saying that if men would work hand in hand, in one combination, there would be a differents state of aflairs in the future. (Applause.) Mr. Crank, of Widnes, and Mr. McCrixx, of Liverpool, also said a few words in support of the resolution, which was afterwards put to the meeting, and carried unani- mously. Votes of thanks to the speakers and Chairman brought the proceedings to a close.

At the annual general meeting of the Society, held re- cently at Hull, the following proposals were unani- mously agreed upon as the basis of a national memorial to the directors of the various railways :—" lst.—That a week's pay be guaranteed to all grades of railway men, who by the terms of their agreement have to devote the whole of their time to the service of the Company em- ploying them. 2nd.—That the maximum hours of duty • be teniper day, excepting platelayers, whose hours, shall .be nine,per day. For shunters in busy goods yards, sig- nalmen at important signal boxes, and boxes always open, eight hours shall be the maximum. In every ease each day's duty to stand by itself, and not be counted as a part of the week's labour. 3rd.—That overtime be paid for at the rate of time and a quarter, and Sunday duty at time and a half."

In the Probate and Divorce Division, on Thursday, the case of lace v. Inca and Hodson ,came before Mr. Justice Butt and a special jury. This was a petition presented by the husband, Dr. Jellin Ince, of the Bengal Medical Service of the Indian Army, praying for the dissolution of his marriage on the ground of the miscon- duct of his wife with theco-respondent, which allegation was denied. The respondent made counter charges against her husband, which he denied. The claim for damages was withdrawn. A decree nisi was granted. LIFE OF MR. PETER RYLANDS.
BY L. GORDON RYLA.NDS, B.A. (Contimued.)

In 1851 Mr. Rylands was appointed Justice of the Peace for the Borough of Warrington, and was tor many years a constant attendant on the Bench. About the same time he was also appointed Justice. of the Peace for the County Palatine of Lancaster In 1833 he was unanimously elected Mayor. His Mayoralty was not destined to be entirely peaceful and without incident, as, during it, two burning questions commuted to make a stir in Warrington —the Footpaths question and the Police question. The first was like a thunder-storm, furious while it lasted, but soon over, or perhaps it would be more appropriate to term it a storm in a tea-cup ; while the latter remained a bone of contention tor years. On the footpath question Mr. Rylands was able to plead his position as Mayor as a ground for remaining neutral, and so escaped some temporary unpopularity which would have fallen upon him had he actively taken the part of those with whom his sympathies lay. In brief, the case was this. 11l 1853 the railway from Stockport to Widnes was completed through Warriegton, cutting certain foot- paths along which the public had a right of way, and particularly a path which led from the town to Arpley Meadows, a favourite resort of the common people on Sundays and holidays. Much excitement was hereby occasioned in the town, and a Footpath Protection Society was formed. As the result of negotiations the Railway Company offered to make a public road along the River Mersey, passimg under- neath the railway and leading to Arpley Meadows, and also to make a level crossing over the railway at the same spot. This simple plan would have increased the distance to be traversed in order to reach the fields by about 200 yards merely. Many leading men in the town, recognising that this scheme met all reasonable objections, and being unwilling to harass the Railway Company, which was likely to be of great service to Warrington, ex- pressed themselves satisfied. But a certain number of unpractical and unreasonable persons worked up the populace into a frenzy by declaring that popular rights were being disregarded, and insisted that a footbridge should be made over the line at the spot where the old path had been cut. This demand was most absurb ; the line is very broad at that point, there being many sidings for shunting goods trains, and the bridge would have to be reached by an ugly and expensive spiral staircase at each end. How- ever, reasoning was powerless, the spark had been applied to the inflammable tinder of popular passion, and the whole town was in a ferment. The excitement was also aggravated by the importation of personal matters into the dispute, for Mr. McMinnies, who was the chief advocate for accepting the Company's offer, had incurred popular displeasure on account of action which he had recently taken in some other matters. Finally, a public meeting was held on February 6th, 1824, to decide the question. The room in which the meeting was held was crowded to suffocation, and hundreds could not gain admittance. Mr. Rylands, as Mayor, presided, and his office was no sinecure, for the meeting was an uproarious one. Mr. McMinnies and Mr. Beamont were howled at, and could with difficulty speak a few sentences between the interruptions. In the end the meeting decided almost unanimously to insist upon the building of a footbridge over the railway. The storm subsided as quickly as it had arisen; the footbridge over the line was made, and proved to be inconvenient as well as unsightly, little use was made of it, a few years later it was quietly removed without a word of protest from anyone, and it is be hoped that those men who had on such a paltry matter stirred up popular animosity against some of the greatest benefactors of the town felt heartily ashamed of them- selves. .. The other question which I mentioned—the Police question—was more serious, and gave rise to a mere protracted struggle. In the year 1854, the police force of Warrington consisted of one chief constable, one inspec- tor, and eight constables, which was a smaller force, in proportion to the number of inhabitants, than existed in any other important town. Constant complaints were received by the Watch Committee and by the magis- trates of assaults and robberies committed with im- punity. The police force, small as it was, was often diminished by the absence of constables with priseners at Kirkdale Gae Land to find a policeman inthe out lying parts of the town at night was almost impossible. Some people employed a private night watchman. Mr. By- lands, asea:magistrate, had become thoroughly alive to this unsatisfactory state of affairs, and, while Mayor, in June, 1854, he succeeded in inducing the Watch Com- , mittee, of which he was a member, to propose an addi- tion of two constables to the police force. Now, I sup- pose there are in all Town Councils and public bodies a certain number of men who endeavour to gain favour with the ratepayers by constant efforts to keep down the rates at any salt. No matter how desirable in itself a proposed reform may be, nor how likely eventually to augment the wealth of the town, such men obstinately oppose it on the ground that it will cause a temporary increase of a penny or so to the rates. And so it was at , Warrington ; and, on the question of the increase of the police force the shorted anti-reformers succeeded in in- , fluencing the Council to such an extent that Mr.Rylands' proposal was defeated by 12 votes to 3. A certainamount of heat was evidently excited by this discussion, and the anti-reformers certainly seemed to be adopting a very defiant attitude when, a few months later, they proposed that the place a a cionstable, who had been discharged for misconduct, should not be filled up, and carried their proposal by 15 votes to 6.. The Warrington police force, which had been quite inadequate before, was now still further weakened, and consisted only of nine men, all told. However, if the obstructionists had their own way for the time being in this matter, in some other directions those who wished to see Warrington progress had been successful, for a new market had been decided upon, and a committee had been formed to superintend its construction, of which Mr. Rylands was chairman. Proposals for a museum and library were being discussed, and in this matter again Mr.Rylands took a leading part. Works were in progress for improving the sewering and widening the streets of the the town ; and schemes for a cemetery were being seriously considered. In fact, War- , ringtou was beginning to wake up. In Icovsnalser, 1854, Mr. Itylands' mayoralty came to aa end. He was urgently requested to continue to hold the office for another year, but was obliged to refuse, owing to the cares of business and many demands upon his time. On this occasion he received the compliment of a public dinner, which was attended by all the principal inhabitants of the neighbourhood, and presided over by Colonel Wilson Patten, who was afterwards raised to the peerage, with a title of Lord Winmarleigh. During the following year the gumboil of the police force remained in an acute stage. Mr. Rylands resigned his seat on the Watch Committee, as he would not be responsible for the orderly government of the town while the force was so small; whereupon the Committee, it would almost seem out of spite, reduced the force still further to seven men. Long discussions on the subject took place at almost every meeting of the Town Couneil, and Mr. Rylands at length succeed in getting the num- ber fixed at the former amount, namely, 10 men in ' all. In 1855, for the first time since 'the incorporation of the borough, the eleetiois of Mayor was not unanimous. This circumstanceswas probably owing partly to per- sonal and partly to political feeling. There was gradu- ally growing up in the Town Council at this time a party of narrow-minded men, who were jealous of the great influence which Mr. Rylands had obtained in the Coun- cil. They could not see that it ;was both natural and even advisable that a man who not only possessed sound common Sel3Bo and greet business ability, but also the power of expressing himself clearly and convincingly, should be a leader in the Council. They refused to recog- nise the abilities by which Mr. Rylands had won for himself so influential a position. They only saw that while his opinion always carried great weight, their was often disregarded in a way that much wounded their self-esteem. They, therefore, declared that Alderman Peter Rylands had got the Town Council under his thumb, and that it was necessary the Council should be emancipated. The election of Mayor seemed to give them their opportunity, and, actuated by a petty jealousy, they determined to strike at Mr. Rylands through his friend, Dr. Hardy, who had been proposed as a candidate. Political feeling also had some force, and Tory Councillors were requested to support Mr. Joseph Chrimes, because he was a Tory. Again, hitherto no shopkeer had been elected as Mayor, and the proposers of Mr. Chrimes excited class prejudices in his favour by saying that there was a conspiracy among the upper classes in the town to keep municipal honours in their own hands, and calling upon shopkeepers in the Council to vindicate the rights of their class by support- ing Mr. Chrimes. The result of all this was, that Mr. Chrimes was elected by lrvotes to 15. This was a most unfortunate election. Hitherto the deliberations of the Town Council had been on the whole harmonious, and the elections of Mayor unanimous. Had the supporters of Mr. Chrimes been willing to make a compromise, that gentleman might have been unanimously elected the fol- lowing year; but nothing could induce them to .forego the 'miserable pleasure of annoying Mr. Rylands, and showing him that "he was not to have things all his own way." Frcm this time there were in the Warrington Town Council two bitterly hostile parties; acrimonious discussions were frequent; sarcastic letters to the " War- rington Guardian" were numerous, and personalities were frequently indulged in. (To be continued.) - trade

. "PETER IT IS ALMOST BEDTIME."

"Gentlemen, lam ninety years old. In the course of nature I must soon depart. Of late it has often seemed to me I could hear my mother's voice, speaking as when I was a boy, and saying, Come, Peter, it is almost bed- time."
At a dinner given in his honour a few weeks before his death, Peter Cooper, the great American philanthro- pist, used the above touching words. "

Pain and suffering sometimes wring from human lips such cries as these : Oh, how I wish I were dead ! " I envy tkose who have got through with this world—and with all its sorrow and misery." Disease makes them talk so. Relieve the pain, cure the torturing ailment, and they enjoy life once more as God intended they should.

Four or five years ago a Canadian woman said to her "how I wish I might die." They received her remark in silence, for they agreed that death alone could deliver her. We can do no more than to hint at what had brought her to this pass. It was the old story —the great and mysterious change from high health to weakness and illness ; up to that date she had been strong and robust. Life had been pleasant to her, and the idea of losing it was repulsive and repellent, as it is to all sound minds in sound bodies. Then came the winter of her discontent. Her head got in the habit of aching; a curious and nauseous taste came into her mouth; the clear white skin turned a yellow or copper-like hue, and she became dull, stupid, and careless about her home duties and affairs. She was often seized with spells of vomiting, and her bowels were costive and irregular. Hitherto this once vigorous woman hardly knew she possessed such an organ as a heart, its beat was so steady, quiet, and true. Now, however, she became aware of it in a way that frightened her. Her heart burned and palpitated at times so violently she could scarcely catch her breath. Her ap- petite failed, and the nerves broke down from want of nourishment. She grew so sensitive to sound and noise that she could not endure the ordinary talk of other members of the family. A few steps further on this road, and the patient usually reaches a condition border- ing on insanity. But this was a sequence and symptom not the disease itself.

In attempting to walk, the poor lady would reel and stagger as though the floor of her room was the deck of a [ship at sea. Her flesh withered away, and left her thin and emaciated. For months she obtained no sleep except under the influence of a narcotic. Her hands and feet were cold owing to the feeble circulation of the blood. The mind was, of course, affected by the state of the body, she was melancholy and low-spirited, and "fears were in the way." Indeed the entire complex being—body and mind—was failing and wasting for the simplest and plainest of all possible reasons,. she could

not retain and digest her food. It is no more than fair to say that she had the benefit of the best medical attention that could be procured. In fact, we are by no means sure that any doctor or doctors in the world could have done more for this unhappy woman than was done by the professional gentlemen who from time to time had charge of the case. Yet they themselves admitted that their labours were without avail. It seemed to them that, as the French cynic said, "a long churchyard sleep" would be the only rest and remedy worth praying for or expecting." Matters were in this dismal sh&pe—when she heard one day of a medicine that was said t 3 have accomplished results quite as surprising as her own restoration to health would certainly be. Without saying a word to ker physician as to her intention, she sent to the nearest large town for a bottle, and began using it secretly. The effect followed so quickly ajter its use, that she could hardly credit her own sensations. The immediate good results were twofold.—She could sleep without the help of drugs, and felt the return of a healthy natural appetite. The body at once felt the impulse of nourish- ment, as the food was no longer thrown up, but was accepted by the stomach and digested. This seemed to answer the question, " What shall I

do ? " Feeling confident what the end would be, she notified her physician that she meant to treat her own case for a while, at least, and then sent for several bot- tles more. She continued the new remedy throughout the whole of the succeeding winter, and with tie return of spring, her health and strength returned. The birds sang not half so sweetly, among the blossoms as joy sang in this rescued woman's heart—Her complaint had been an obstinate attack of indigestion and dyspep- sia, and the victorious medicine was Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. We shall be glad to send this lady's name and address to any one who desires to verify this statement ; she is now about sixty-five years of age, and enjoys her life too much to wish to leave it before kindly nature's distant bedtime.

div.head: TILE O'SHEA.-PARNELL DIVORCE CASE.
div.p: TILE O'SHEA.-PARNELL DIVORCE CASE.
WITEIDRAWAL OF _THE DEFENCE.

In the Divorce Division on Saturday, Mr. Justice Butt and a special jury had before them the case of O'Shea V. O'Shea and Parnell. The petition was that of Captain William Henry O'Shea, a J.P. in the county Clare, for a divorce by reason of the alleged adultery of his wife, Mrs. Catherine O'Shea, with Mr. Charles Stewart Parnell, M.P. Answers were filed denying the charge, and the respondent made counter-allegations against her husband which he denied. Mrs. Steele is an intervener in the nase.—The Solioitor General (Sir E. Clarke, Q.C.), Mr. Inderwiek, Q.C., and Lewis Coward appeared for Captain O'Shea ; mid Mr. Lockwood, Q.C., and Mr. Pritchard for the respondent. Mr. Parnell was not re- presented bycounsel, but Mr. George Lewis, his solicitor, was present. Mr. M'Call appeared for the intervener. came into court with his son shortly bCeafpetraeinha?fSlie half-past ten.—Mr. Coward, in opening the plead- ings, said that there was a charge of connivance, neglect, and conduct conducive to the adultery and wilful separa- tion ; further, that the petitioner had been guilty of un- reasonable delay, also of cruelty. The petitioner denied the several allegations.—Mr. Lockwood, Q.C., before the ease was opened, said that he appeared for Mrs. O'Shea, and he was instructed on her behalf to say that he did not intend to cress-examine any of the witnesses or to take any part in the proceedings.—The Solicitor said that the announcement of his learned friend had seriously altered the position of the affairs.—Mr. Justice Butt: Is there anyone appearing for Mr. Parnell? There was no answer.—The Solicitor General then stated the case, and reed a number of letters which had passed between the parties. In one of these,dated in 1331, Cap- tain O'Shea challenged Mr. Parnell to fight a duel on the Continent. In 1888 he invited Mr. Parnell to dine at his house. The petitioner was absent from home for long periods, and it was shown that Mr. Parnell was often in the respondent's company, and that they occupied the same house at Eastbourne for many weeks. The respon- dent had made counter-charges against the petitioner, but these were withdrawn. Evidence having been given by.the servants in, Mr. O'Shea's house, the further hear- ing of the suit was adjourned. DIVORCE GRANTED.

On Monday evening the hearing of the O'Shea divorce case was resumed, before Mr. Justice Butt and a special jury, neither Mr. Parnell nor Mrs. O'Shea being present, Jane Glannister, who was in the service of Mrs. O'Shea at One Ash Lodge, from October, 1880, till October, 1882, stated that soon after entering the service she saw Mr. Parnell at Eltham, where he remained for two or three days, and slept in the house, Captain O'Shea being there also. In May, 1881, Mrs. O'Shea returned from a visit to Brighton, and Mr. Parnell came a great deal, occupying a bedroom separated by a dressing-room from Mrs. O'Shea's bedroom, communications existing between the two bedrooms without going on to the landing. On one occasion witness knew Mr. Parnell and Mrs. O'Shea to be together in the drawing-room with the door locked, Mrs. O'Shea explaining that "the Secret Society was about, and it was necessary for the door to be locked." Every night that Mr. Parnell came to Eltham after the rising of Parliament Mrs. O'Shea used be come down stairs and join him. Witness was instructed to say "No " if anyone asked if Mr. Parnell was there. Richard Wise, the coachman, and Thomas Partridge, a stable helper, gave evidence as to Mr. Parnell visiting Mrs. O'Shea at Eltham and Eastbourne. Mr. Ernest Viell, house agent and surveyor, Eastbourne, gave evidence as to Mr. Parnell taking a house from him in thename of Campbell, being at the same time accompanied by Mrs. O'Shea. A number of other witnesses gave evidence of an incrimina- tory character, and afterwards Mrs. Steele entered the box and indignantly repudiated the charge of having committed adultry with Captain O'Shea. The latter was afterwards interrogated by a juryman regarding the allegation of neglect, but he denied emphatically that he had ever neglected his wife, or that she had complained. The judge, in summing up, slid the charge of adultery with Mrs. Steele alleged against Captain O'Shea was simply shocking, and there did not appear to be the the slightest foundation for it. He should not trouble the jury with this charge. The jury, without leaving the box, found that Mr. Parnell and. Mrs. O'Shea had com- mitted adultery, and that there had been no connivance on the part of Captain O'Shea. His Lordship pronounced a decree nisi, and condemned the co-respondent in costs, some minor questions being left for discussion in chambers.

div.head: GUN-MAKER OF MOSCOW;
div.p: THE GUN-MAKER OF MOSCOW;
OR, VALDIMIR THE MONK.
BY SYLVANUS COBB, Jn.
CHAPTER V.
THE DUEL.

On the following morning Ruric was up betimes, and at the breakfast table not a word of the one all- absorbing theme was uttered. After the meal was finished the gun-maker went out of his shop and took down from one of the closets a long leathern case, in which were two swords, both of the same make and finish, only different in size. They were Toledo blades, and of most exquisite workmanship and finish. Runic took out the heaviest one, which was a too-edged weapon with a cross-hilt of heavily gilded metal, lie placed the point upon the floor and then, with all his weight, he bent the blade till the pommel touched the point. The lithe steel sprang back to its place with s sharp clang, and the texture was not started. Then he struck the flat of the blade upon the anvil with great force. The ring was sharp and clear, and the weapon remained un- harmed.
"By St. Michael, Paul, Moscow does not contain another blade like that. Damascus never saw a better."

Thus spoke the gun-maker to his boy as he bal- anced the beautiful weapon in his band. "I think you are right, my master," the boy re- turned, who had beheld the trial of the blade with 1 unbounded admiration. But," he added, " could you not temper a blade like that ?" "Perhaps, if I had the steel. But I have not. The steel of these two blades came from India, and was originally in one weapon—a ponderous, two-handed affair, belonging to a Bengal chieftain. The metal possesses all the hardness of the finest razor, with the elasticity of the most subtle spring. My old master at Toledo gave me these as a momento. Were Ito mention the sum of money he was once offered for the largest one you would hardly credit it." "low much ? " asked Paul, with a boy's curiosity.
, "It was a sum equal to about seven hundred ducats."

"And yet he gave it away." "Aye—for its price was but imaginary, while its worth to him was only commensurate with the good it did him. If he told the truth he loved me, and these he gave me as a parting gift, as the best pat- terns I could wish for when making such." After this Rune put up -a small sword, and then he gave Paul a few directions about the work, prom- ising to be back before night. The faithful boy shook his head dubiously as he heard this promise, but he said nothing, and shortly afterwards Ruric went into the house. Just then Alaric Orsa drove up to the d00r... . .
Rune was all ready but putting on his bonnet and pelisse. His mother was in the kitchen. He went to her with a smile upon his face. He put his arms about her and drew her to his bosom.

"God bless you, ',my mother! I shall come back." He said this, and then kissed her. "God keep—and—" It was all she could say. Ituric gazed a moment into her face--then he kissed her again—and again he said: " God bless you, my mother! I shall come back." He dared not stop to speak more. Gently seating his fond motherupon a chair, be turned and hurried from the place. In the ball he threw on his pelisse and bonnet, and then he opened the door and passed out. "Have you a good weapon? " asked Orsa, as the horse started on.

"I have a fair one. I think it will not deceive me," returned Ruric. "I asked," resumed Orsa, " because Damonoff prides himself upon the weapon he wears. It is a German blade, and he thinks he can cut in twain the blade of any other weapon in Moscow with

"I have a good weapon,'' Ruric said quietly; "and one which has stood more tests than most swords will bear." And after some further remarks he related the peculiar circumstances attending the making of the sword, and his possession of it.

At length they struck upon the river, and in half an hour more they reached the appointed spot. The day was beautiful. The sun shone brightly upon the glistening snow, and the air was still and calm. Ths sharp frost of the atmosphere served only to braoe the system up, and Ruric threw open his pelisee that he might breathe more freely. He had been upon the ground but a few minutes when the other party came in sight around the head of the river.

As soon as the Count and his second arrived, and the horses had been secured,the lieutenant proposed that they should repair to the building which was close at hand. This was a large open boat house, which was unwed and deserted in the winter, and it was proposed to go in there beeause the reflection of the strong sunlight from the bright snow was calculated to blind and blur the eye. "Ha I what means that ?" uttered Orsa,as he saw a sledge just turning the bend of the river with an officer in it. _ _
"it is only a surgeon," replied Damonoff. "I would not cut a man's flesh without giving him a fair chance to survive it."

"And then you may find him serviceable to your- self, eh ?" suggested the lieutenant. "Of course. There is no telling what may happen." In a monent more the new sledge came up, and Rune recognised its inmate as an army surgeon whom he had seen before; though he knew not his name. "Now for the old boat house," cried Urzen. "Aye," added Damonoff. "Let us have this business done, for I would be back to dinner. I dine with Olga to-day, and a fair maiden awaits my coming." "Notice him not," whispered Orsa, who walked close by Rune's side. " That is one of his chief points when engaged in an affair of this kind. He hopes to get you angry, and so unhinge your nerves."

"Never fear." returned the gun-maker. "Be sure he only brings new danger to himself, for such efforts will find their point in the muscle of my arm." The party halted when they reached the interior of the rough structure, and the Count throw off his pelisse and drew his sword. Marie followed his example. s Sir Count,* the latter said, as he moved a step forward. "ere we commence this work, I wish all present, to understand distinctly how I stand. You have sought this quarrel from the first. With- out the least provocation from me, you have in- sulted me most grossly, and this is the climax. So, before God and man, be the result upon your own head."

' out, lying knave—" "Hold," cried the surgeon, laying his hand heavily upon the Count's arm. You have no rOlt to speak thus, for you lower yourself when you do it. If you have come to fight, do so bocourabl:i':" An angry reply was upon Damom.ff's lips, but 110 did not speak it. lie turned to his alii.agol ist and said: "Will you measure weapon-, sir? 'Mine may be a mite the longest. I seek no advantage; and I have one here of the same length and weight as my own if you wish it." "I am well satisfied as it is," replied Runic. "Then take your ground. Are you ready ?" " I am 1" The two swords were crossed in an instant, with a clear, sharp clang. There was some contrast between the two com- batants, but not much apparently, The Count was a little the taller and Rune was somewhat heavier. But to a close observer there was a peculiar con- trast in the bearing of the two men. That breast swelling out so nobly, and those massive shoulders, made for the seat of physical power, were Ruric's alone to possess. Yet Conrad Damonoff was ac- counted a strong man. In the athletic sports of the court-club he had few superiors, and not many equals. But Runic Nevel had never shown his strength there. Now, for the first time, that contemptuous look passed from the Count's face. As his eye caught his antagonist's position—as he noticed the calm, dignified, quiet ease of every limb; and as he caught the deep, mystic fire of those expressive eyes, he knew that he had no common amateur to deal with. _ _

At length Conrad Damonoff started back, and a quick cry escaped his lips. His antagonist's point had touched his bosom—it had pressed against his heart, and had .not been driven home. Well he knew that his life was his no longer, for the gun- maker had gained it, and—spared it. " You fence well," he gasped, struggling to regain his composure. "You are not a novice," returned Runic calmly, at the same time allowing his point to drop.

"Come on," the Count uttered, now gathering all his energies for another effort. And again the weapons were crossed. This time Damonoff was more guarded. Before he had been impelled by his own assurance; but now he was forced to regard his opponent's power. R uric quicklY. found that the other was mere careful than the first, and he carried his own point accordinglY• .At the twelfth stroke the Count made a feint to the left—then at the throat, and then, with a quick,' lightning-like motion, he brought his point to hi; antagonist's heart. But his meaning had been rean from the first by Ruric. The youth caught the motion of the eye, and he saw that his heart was the place looked to. His own movement was almosat instinctive. He received his antagonist's swot midway upon his own blade—then moved his arin quickly forward and caught the point under his, cross-guard—then, with all his power, he wrenche,a his arm upward and backward, and the Cowl" sword went fly across the building. It struck the opposite wall with a dull' clang, and the next in— stant it was half buried in the snow. " Fear not, sir," said Runic, as the Count started back with both hands raised, " I never strike an unarmed man." Damonoff's arms fell to his side, and a deep blush of shame mantled his face. "By St. Paul," cried the surgeon, " your life is forfeited, sir Count ; and now you should be satis- fied." " No, no," the discomfited man exclaimed, start; ing up with rage and mortification. "That was, hll,, a slip. 'Twits a false step—a cowardly feint. i a"" not overcome." "But, man of mortality, even now your life is Nevel's. he may run you through now if 114 chooses." "But he has not," the Count cried, springing t'° where his sword had fallen, and snatching it UPS "Sir Count," here spoke Rune calmly, but Nvi: r marked contempt," you should not blame me what I have done, for thrice you have tried to brew, my sword." "Then try it again ! " Damonoff returned. " Take my sword again if you can." " Perhaps not, our hero retorted. " But be your sword shall be used no more after this daY•

" Ha! Brag not, but strike. If you can—" The conclusion of the sentence was drowned "J the clash of steel. At the second stroke the Count made another furious thrust at his antagonist's heart. I{urier sprang quickly aside, and with the whole powe, of his good right arm he struck Damonoff's blade close to the haft and broke it in twain. " My other sword ! ray other sword ! " the Count shouted, now blinded by absolute madness. " give me my other—" "Hold 1 " cried both the surgeon and Stephen Urzen in concert. `• You are mad, Conrad." " Mad ?—Oh, I shall go mad ! Where is nIY. sward the reckless man yelled, casting the blade- less pommel down. "But will you not listen one—" "Away, I say ! Shall I give up because my esv°r is broke? By the gods, the weapon deceived rue' Where is the other ?" "Deceived thee, Conrad?" repeated the surgeon' sarcastically. "By the holy Host! had thy heaccil but received a hundredth part of the blow, 'twoul not be upon thy shoulders now.' 4 But the Count was beyond all reason. In his madness he saw not that his sword had been broken on purpose. He did not see that he had been at his antagonist's mercy. But his friends saw it all. " Ha ! whom have we here ?" cried Alaric, Nvho9° eye had caught a dark form at the entrance of the old building. It was Valdimir the monk. " How now? What seek ye here ?" asked Urzen, as the fat, burly monk waddled towards the party'. " I heard the clash of arms, my son, as I rode by.' and I stopped to see what it was. Surely, will: the work of death is going on a child of the Wu church of God may come." "Aye," cried me Count, "Come in and welcoro,!,. ' but meddle not. Now I—my sword !—where is it An Reluctantly Urzen brought forward the soo°tl' sword, but ere he gave it up he said : " Beware, Conrad. You had better—" " Peace, babbler !" the excited fool hissed, enat'eb- ing the weapon, and then turning quickly upon the gun-maker. Thus far Ruric had remained silent, but he felt his duty to speak now. "Sir Count," he said, in a tone so stern and authoritative, and with a look so commanding, that! the other was held in abeyance by it," I must speak one word. You have provoked a quarrel with fl and you have challenged me. I have no fear of death when duty calls for my life, but I would no; die thus, nor would I slay a fellow-being thus. Six separate times to-day, since our swords first crossed, have I spared your life—" " Liar !"

—"And twice have I had you before me un- armed," Ruric continued, without noticing the inter- ruption. " I had hoped this would have shoWn you that I sought not to harm yen; and, furthelw more, that you were no match for me at this kind of work." "Out, fool !" yelled Damonoff,now fairly frothing with rage. "If you dare not cross swords Wing say so ; but do not crawl off like a coward!" ' One word more," uttered Ruric, paling for an instant beneath the unmerciful insult of the sense- less tongue that assailed him—and he stood proudly erect while he spoke—" before these men here assembled and before my God, I swear that thus far have I spared you; but my ow° life may be the forfeit if I trifle with you more. So now—beware! You have sufficient warn- ing !" Perhaps the Count really overlooked the fasts of which Rude had spoken. In his ungovernable Nage he may have fancied that 'twas only accident th ,sht • had worked against him. However, he starw'r • forward once more, and male a furious lunge at hi° antagonist. "Now," he grasped, "play your best, for WI sword's my own ! But Runic spoke not. He saw that the Ooltns was stronger than before—for his rage seemed tie give him a maniac's power—and that he was earn" est only for life or death. He struck quickly and, furiously, and his move,ments were strange soil unprecedented. He threw up all rules of exercise., and cut and thrust only in wild madness. Twice Ruric came nigh beihg run through. He lost all run of his opponent's play, and quickly saw the' he must put a stop to the conflict or run the risk of leaving a childless mother in his home to see tbst day's sun sink. "Will you give o'er ?" he asked, as he struck gig' Count's point down. " Never ! Submit to such as you? Bah !” A few moments more the conflict lasted. One' more opportunity he had at Damonoff's hear and he spared him. All present saw it except the mad man.

" Fool !" uttered the monk, who trembled fro,Dl ' head to foot with excitement, his huge belly alaal'' lug like a bag of jelly, "will you throw away Yotir own life, Ruric Neve] ? Shall I tell your mother you left her of your own will?" This mention of his mother called the last linger- ing doubt from Rune's mind. Again he struck the opposing point down, and then he pressed his own point upon the Count's bosom. He avoided the heart—he tried to avoid the vitals—but be threw his arm forward, and his glittering blade passed throug,b the fool's body. With an expression ef pain uvon his features he started back, and rested his reeking point upon the trodden snow. Tha Count came furiously on again, but he struck wildly, and at random, Rnrie merely warding off his blows, until finally his arm sank. On the ne-xt moment his sword fell trom his nerveless grasp, and he sank fainting back into the arms of his attendants.
(To be eontinued.)

div.head: HORRIBLE TRAGEDY NEAR BOLTON.
div.p: HORRIBLE TRAGEDY NEAR BOLTON.

A SCHOOLMISTRESS MURDERED. ARREST OF A RETURNED CONVICT. The neighbourhood of Bolton was startled on Saturday 3light by the discovery of a shocking tragedy, the sur- roundings of which left no doubt that a horrible murder had been committed. The victim was Miss Elizabeth -Ann Holt, aged 21, the younger of two daughters of a "Widow living in Darwen-road, Dunscar. She was a par- ticularly refined and attractive young woman, engaged ae a schoolmistress at Belmont, between three or, four Mileedistant from her home. She was in the habit of returning home each Friday night and remaining until -Monday morning, lodging during the week with Mr. ilwayles, the schoolmaster. On Monday week, the 10th inst., she left home about 7.30 a.m. to proceed to school. Bile never arrived, and the schoolmaster, concluding that she was unwell, did not communicate with the Mother, who on her part thought her daughter was at school. When Miss Holt did not return home on Friday evening some anxiety was created, and, on Saturday _Morning, her sister went to Belmont to make inquiries. NO trace could there be found, and the sister returned to bengworth Hall Farm, a place about midway. On in- quiring there she was told that the deceased had passed as usual on Monday. The fact of her disappearance re- ▪ ded one of the sons that he had seen an umbrella ling in Longworth Clough. A search was then insti- tuted, and other articles were found, together with de- Teased's hat, scarf, and basket containing provisions. On further search, marks of a struggle were observed, and, ultimately, the body of the unfortunate girl was discovered lying at the bottom of a steep descent, in a running stream of water. She was entirely covered with leaves and bracken ; and but for the mound thus made 'Would have been passed unnoticed. On removing the debris a shocking sight presented itself. The poor girl's throat was cut from the centre round to the back on tbe left side, in a most inhuman manner. Her clothes werd torn and disarranged, and she had evidently been lying there a week. Decomposition was not much advanced, the running water having preservedthe corpse. With all baste the police were communicated with, and the multi- lated body conveyed home. Dr. Robinson, of Dunscar, tuade a superficial examination of the body, and gave it as his opinion that deceased had been pursued and fainted, and that the throat was cut whilst unconscious ,- and she was dragged when dead down the declivity. He did not think an outrage was perpetrated, although prior to the port-mortem he could not speak positively. ARREST OF A RETURNED CONVICT. The greatest excitement prevails in the district. The body was discovered at 4.30, and less than four hours later, Sergeant Hayward, of the county police,had made arresC The prisoner was Thomas M'Donald, labourer, a, of 244, Blackburn-road, Egerton, not far from the scene of the murder. M'Donald has a bad record. In 1882 he was sentenced to ten years penal servitude for a rape perpetrated in the same locality. He was re- leased on ticket-of-leave in April last. On the 13th Sep- tember a young man named Thomas Mather was found drowned in Dunscar Lodge. M'Donald was proved to have been the last person in his company, and he was arrested on suspicion. There was no evidence beyond that against him, however, and the Coroner's jury ac- quitted him, on the 24th September. On the Monday, When the murder must have been committed, he was arrested for being drunk and disorderly, and was fined 10s. And costs for the offence on Thursday, being allowed tune to pay. On Monday morning he was seen following deceased through the fields within a few hundred yards of where the body was discovered. Several witnesses speak to this, and, on his arrest, he admitted it, adding, however, that he did no harm. Prior to his arrest on Monday he pawned a finger ring, which the police think Will be proved to have belonged to deceased. On a pre, wious occasion he had followed her, and she turned back. In his possession, when arrested, was an ordinary clasp knife, the blade of which was stained and discoloured, but, with what has not yet been ascertained. On Sunday the scene of the awful discovery was visited by hundreds of persons. Two of the witnesses to speak to M'Donald following deceased on the Monday morning are Robert Simpson and John Talbot, farmers' sons, working in the fields in the neighbourhood. One of them remarked to the other at the time—" Why, that's, the chap that was brought UP for that drowning case." Five hundred yards further en the body was found. In custody M'Donald betrays no uneasiness. He is atlort of statue, dark, with piercing eyes, and a promin- ent nose. During the drowning incjairy he distinguished himself by shrewd cross-examination of the witnesses. THE PRISONER IN COURT. On Monday the scene of the tragedy attracted con- siderable streams of visitors, and feeling was runninu high in the neighbourhood, not only against the prisoner, out also against his aunt, who worked at some cotton Mills in the neighbourhood, and with whom he lived. She was compelled to leave her employ, as the other 'lands refused to remain with her. She has also, received notice to quit her cottage. ...The inquest was opened at Turton, on Monday, by °tr. Butcher, county coroner, and after evidence of identification by the mother, Mrs. Holt, a widow, who Was prostrated with grief, was adjourned until Saturday, when it will be resumed at Bolton. M'Donald, the supposed murderer, was placed in the dock on Monday morning, and Superintendent Eatough, after stating that the charge was "wilful murder," ap- Riled for a remand until Thursday.—The prisoner said, I see no reason why I should not be tried now, so long 461 PIII not guilty; none at all."—The remand was granted. It has transpired that the deceased had seven-and-six- Pence in her possession, which is missing ; and, on Mon- p,y week, the prisoner, who is out of work, was treating nns companions. The ring he pawned is a worthless article which has no connection with the murder. The girl's friends fail to identify it as her property. Shortly after nine o'clock on the morning of the minder the pn- !loner asked a carter for a match, and the carter noticed that he was trembling violently. On the Thursday night his movements were so peculiar that the police set a Watch on him. Strange stories are circulated as to his antecedents. On the night of the drowning case at Duns- ear, in connection with which the prisoner was arrested „i suspicion, he went home and broke the furniture. Seeing a canary in a cage, he said, "11l teach thee to start at me !" and put it on the fire. On another occasion he nearly strangled a companion by tightening his scarf Mita he cc as black in the face. When arrested eight Years ago, he said to his aunt, "Get me some bacca. It's the last I shall have for ten years." THE DOCTOR'S STATEMENT. An important statement has been made by Dr. 140binson, who made the post-mortem examination of Uie body of the deceased. He says that the girl was not violated, though there had evidently been an attempt Made. The murderer appears in his rage to have re- Peatedly kicked his victim, as the skull is literally 'numbed in. Kicks were the cause of death, but the man then cut her throat on the left side, the weapon entering, the front of the throat and cutting right through arteries and everything right down to the spine. There was also a stab at the top of the head, and wounds on the temple. tlia perpetrator must have been a maniac at the time of the murder. A PREVIOUS VICTIM'S EXPERIENCE. The prisoner M'Donald still maintains a calm and im- perturbable demeanour. On Monday he was examined by the doctor, who discovered a number of cuts and Scratches on his hands, which might have been inflicted by a weapon such as is supposed to have been used to cut deceased's throat. The stains on his clothing have IflCit yet been analysed, the police analyst being away tom home. Mrs. Harwood, of Darwen, who, when a single woman eight years ago, was criminally assaulted 17 prisoner, says that since his release he has haunted tier house and threatened to "do for her." In conse- rence she had never left home without protection. nuPerintendent Eatough is making inquiries in a direc- tion which it is said will throw much light on the case. A startling rumour comes from the Globe Inn, Egerton, where a customer is reported to have said, that on the Saturday prior to the murder, Macdonald boasted that a Belmont schoolmistress was afraid of him, and that he 'Would kiss and squeeze her within a fortnight. FUNERAL OF THE VICTIM. A sympathetic crowd assembled in the village of Eger- ton, to witness the funeral of Miss Holt. The body was interred in the family grave, at Walmsley Church, the key. J. Stott officiating. The tomb, her last resting-place, [lad only been opened a few weeks ago to receive the grandmother of the murdered lady. The coffin was liter- ati,' covered with wreaths, the loving tokens of many 'friends, one bearing the inscription, "From her true and loving George, with heart-broken sympathy and love." This came from a young gentleman at Birmingham. The Scholars at Eagley School, formerly taught by Miss Holt, the schoclmaster and schoolmistress at Belmont, and numerous relatives and friends attended the funeral, and the churchyard was densely crowded. The greatest in- terest continues to be manifested in the murder and its Pessible developments, and intense excitement prevails in the district. The hearse and carriages were provided gratuitously by Messrs. Holden and Co , and the utmost aYmpathy was exhibited onevery hand. The young man from Birmingham who sentthe wreath attended the funeral of the victim. His name is Cooper, and he is a jeweller. He says he never gave Miss Holt a ring, nor knew her to wear one, so that the ring pledged by the prisoner has evidently nothing to do with the case. Though the shirt Macdonald wore on the fatal Monday 15 missing, what is believed to be his waistcoat was found early on Wednesday morning, hidden behind a wall on a road leading to the scene of the murder. The prisoner M'Donold was on Wednesday night brought from his cell at the Bolton County Police Court and formerly charged by Police-sergeant Hayward with the terrible murder of Miss Holt, in Longworth Wood. Tie replied that he had nothing to say. Mr. Brown, county analyst, has submitted the pri- soner's clothes for examination by the eminent specia- list, Dr. Paull, of Liverpool, who hopes to be ready for the inquest on Saturday. The prisoner's right hand has been photographed. The police state that they have accumulated a mass of evidence, and are confident that they will be able to convince the jury tbas it was morally bnpossible for any one else to commit the murder except tile prisoner.

STARTLING DISCOVERIES. On Thursday morning a shopkeeper at Egerton found a blood-stained shirt sleeve hanging on a tree neer the entrance to Ashworth's works, where the prisoner M,Donald went to see his aunt on the morning of the murder. The sleeve is of cotton material similar to that worn by the prisoner. The police now think the mur- derer got in front of the decased girl near Longworth Hall Farm, and proceeded by the lower pathway to the place where he pounced on her. The primer's defence iS expected to be that oaths mornina of the tragedy he had secured work at a coal shaft at Belmont, and, that he would have gone there by thisparticular route. PRISONER AGAIN BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES. , M'Donald was again before the magistrates at the County Police Court, Bolton, on Thursday. Intense ex- citement was manifested by the public in the proceed- ings, and long before the hour fixed for the holding of the court, the precincts were thronged with a crowd clamouring for admission. Prisoner seemed to feel the gravity of his position, and stared mind with an anxious gaze. Mr. John Hall, who has been instructed to prose- cute on behalf of the Treasury, addressing the justices said: The prisoner• Thomas M'Donald is charged with the wilful murder of Elizabeth Ann Holt, at Longworth, near Bolton, on the 10th inst. The case has been before the court on a previous occasion,when the circumstances attending the crime were detailed. It is, therefore, un- necessary for me to make any further statement. My application is that the prisoner should be remanded until Monday, when, in au probability, the police will have finished inquiries which they are now making. The Chairman: Our own feeling is that asthe case was before us on Monday, and remanded without any evidence having been taken, we think it proper that a certain amount of evidence should be put forward to justify a further demand. Mr. Hall At this stage, I repeat, that I don't propose to offer you any evidence. The prisoner: I don't wish the case to go forward until I am provided with proper clothing, as mine has been taken away. The Chairman: Then you would rather have a remand? Yes, as long as I have no proper clothes. The case was thereupon adjourned until Monday.
