div.head: CURE OF CONSUMPTION.
div.p: THE CURE OF CONSUMPTION.

DR. KOCH'S DISCOVERY. In an extraordinary edition of the German "Medical Weekly." Dr. Koch publishes an articleentitled," Further communications regarding a Cure of Tuberculosis, and the experiments relating thereto, performed by Dr. Libbertz and Staff-Surgeon Dr. Pfuhl, under the direc- tion of Dr. Koch." Respecting the derivation and pre- paration of the matter employed, Dr. Koch can as yet give no indications, as his work is not yet completed. The matter itself is, however, to be obtained from Dr. Libbertz, whose address is 28, Lueneburger, Strasse, Berlin. It consists of a brownish transparent liquid which is by its own properties proof against deterioration. NOW APPLIED. The curative matter does not operate through the stomach, and therefore has tobe applied sub-cutaneously. Dr. Koch has used for this purpose a syringe, which has commended itself to him by his bacteriological experi- ments, having no valve, and furnished only with a small hollow ball of indiarubber, the merit of this syringe being that it can be easily and surely rinsed out with absolute alcohol and kept in an aseptic condition. With more than a thousand sub-cutaneous injections not a single abscess has occurred. The places selected for applying the injection are the skin of the back between the shoulder blades, and in proximity to the loins. SOME EFFECTS OF TUB INJECTIONS. The lowest limit of effective strength in the healthy human body is 0-01 cubic centimetres, showing little or no reaction. The same is the case with deceased persons suffering from other than tuberculous affections. But in persons attacked with tuberculosis, the same dose pro- duces a strong reaction, both general and local. The former consists in an attack of fever mostly commencing with a shivering fit, and the temperature of the body then rises to over 39, and even up to 41 degrees centi- grade. At the same time pains in the limbs are notice- able, together with cough-irritation and great exhaus- tion, and sometimes nausea and vomiting. In somecases there is a slight icteric colouring or .exanthema, resem- bling measles, on the chest or neck. As a rule, this attack commences about four or five hours, after the injection, and its duration is from twelve to fifteen hours. The patient is but little affected by the attack. The second, or local, reaction can best be observed in individuals whose tubercular affection is visible, as with those suffering from lupus. The remedy may be con- sidered for the future as an indispensable auxiliary to diagnosis whereby doubtful cases of incipient phthisis itself can be diagnosed if positive information regarding the- nature of the disease is not to be obtained. CURATIVE PROPERTIES OT! THE REMEDY. Affecting the glands, latent tuberculosis of the bones, doubtful skin tuberculosis, etc., can be easily, and with certainty ascertained to be such. In cases of lung or joint tuberculosis which have apparently passed off it will be possible to establish as a fact whether the morbid process has in reality been brought to an absolute end. But of still greater importance than for the purposes of diagnosis are the curative properties of the remedy. What it kills is not the tubercular bacillus, but the tubercular tissue,and this gives us the well defined limits to which the efficaciousness of the remedy will go. It can only influence living tuberculous tissue, but does not ' affect the dead tissues (decayed caseous matter, necrotic bones, &c.), nor those tissues which have been killed by the application of the remedy itself. It is quite possible that on such masses of dead tissue there are still living tuberculous bacilli, which are then either expelled with the necrotic tissue, or may, perhaps, under special cir- cumstances, again invade the adjacent and still living tissues. Therefore, continually increased doses are re- quired to obtain the same degree of reaction as before. SIGNS OF A CURL As soon as the tuberculosis patients have been so far treated with increasing doses that there is as little reac- tion with them as with non-tuberculous people, it may be assumed that all the tuberculous tissue open to re- action is dead. Whether this interpretation and these conclusions, says Dr. Koch, are correct, the future will say, but for the present they are convincing to him. DATA CONCERNING THE REMEDY. Dr. Koch, in conclusion gives the following date re- garding the application hitherto of the remedy lupus patients had been sufferers from the disease for many years, and had hitherto peen treated by other means without result. Sufferers from tuberculosis of the lymphatic glands, bones, and joints have been treated with precisely the same success as the lupus cases. Con- sumptives have almost invariably shown strong reaction on considerably reduced doses. One can afterwards an- vance to those quantities which can be easily borne by other patients. Thus a patient can be brought to take very high doses almost without fever, and almost imper- ceptibly to himself. Consumptives who are still fairly strong have reached the increased doses quicker, and favourable results have apparently followed with cor- responding rapidity. Patients treated in the early stage of phthisis have one and all been freed from all morbid symptoms within four to six weeks, and may be re- garded as healed. Cases of relapse are, of course, for the present, not impossible, although it is lust as possible that persons once cured are cured for good.

div.head: LOSS OF H.M.S. SERPENT.
div.p: THE LOSS OF H.M.S. SERPENT.
EVIDENCE OF SURVIVORS.

• The following telegram has been received by the Ad- miralty, from the commanding officer of her Majesty's ship Lapwing, dated Corcubion, November 15th "Serpent total wreck five miles north of Cape Villano; masthead just visible in trough of heavy sea now run- ning ; three survivors • list five, No. 148, Edwin Burton, AU., of Camberwell, London ; list five,No. 42,Frederick Joseph Gould, leading seaman, of Egg Backland, Devon- shire ; list five. No. 17, Oney Luxon, A. 8., of Quay Topsham, near Exeter. Latter two slight flesh wounds, doing well ; all remainder perished. Thirty-three bodies washed ashore; 21 buried; propose bury remainder military honours. Survivors state ship struck 10.30 p.m. Monday, 10th, steering S. by W., three-quarters W, nine not ; weather thick and wet, force 8; violent heavy swell; thumping on rock about half an hour; officers remained on bridge; ship's company took to rigging by order of captain. A tre- mendous sea then struck her and threw her on bean% ends ; the three survivors, being lifeboat's crew, had belts on, vere washed overboard, and could state nOthing further with accuracy. Wounded have been visited by surgeon of this ship. Am just going to visit scene of wreck; will wire further details; have wired relatives of survivors." The following telegram was received later i•—• " Visited wreck twice, at high and low water. Nothing visible, though only 150 yards from shore at low water. Much surf; not much wreckage and that valueless. Request instructions disposal. Forty-five bodies re- covered, including Captain Ross and Engineer W. P. Edwards. Decently buried in enclosure on beach; arrangements made to consecrate same with local clergy. Take wounded men hospital to-morrow Corunna. Funeral service performed by me when ground conse- crated. Am surveying scene of wreck." BODIES WASHED ASHORE.

TAIIIRSDAY.—Her Majesty's ship Tyne has not yet left here for England with the survivors of the Serpent, but is expected to sail immediately. Bodies continue to be thrown up on the beach at Camarinas, and the number buried in the specially formed cemetery is now fifty-six. The proposal to station a lightship off Cape Finisterre is the outcome of opinions expressed by the survivors of numerous vessels wrecked off the Galician , coast in consequence of their compasses having been dis- turbed. A siren foghorn is sounded from the Cape Finisterre Lighthouse in thick weather, but it was use- less to prevent the loss of the Derwentwater. The sur- vivors of that steamer have reached here, and are await- ing the arrivaAl ol‘aANfi The Lord Mayor of London yesterday received a steamer SIO N Htomi cosnEvelymND. letter from the Duke of Edinburgh, asking him to open a subscription at the Mansion House in connection with the Serpent fund. His lordship has consented to do so.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 22, 1890.
LACROSSE.

WARRINGTON v. SALE. This match was played at Arpley, on Saturday last. Shortly after three the centres faced and the visitors going off with a rush scored after a few minutes' play. The home team were without three of their defence men and this soon told its tale, and in the first ten minutes Sander- son an old county man, who played a splendid game, scored three times. Not until the mischief had been done did the home team realise their position, when a change of places checked the.scoring. Still the visitors., led by , Sanderson notched another goal. The home attacks now warnied to their work, Bennett and Smith making indi- vidual efforts to defeat the opposing defence. Garnett made a good run on the right wing and had hard lines in not sconng, and at half-time the game was in favour of the visitors by four goals to none. Flom the reface War- rington played up well and one of their homes managed to put the ball through the posts. This roused the visi- tors, and the home defence worked hard and, after 'some even play, the Warrington left attack took a smart pass and shot a beatiful goal. After this the Sale men tried hard to score, but the Warrington defence was now good and kept them at bay. Time was shortly afterwards called, leaving Sale the winners of an extremely pleasant game by four goals to two. Warrington had much the best of the game in the second half, but would not score as they ought to have done, missing some easy chances only putting on two goals. The visitors played a smart combined game their picking up and passing being very good. Warrington team : Goal, Barker; point, Garnett junior; cover-point, Wilson ; third-man, Dunn; left de- fence, Parry ; right defence, Garnett; centre, Bennett; right attack, Tetlow ; left attack, Jones ; third-home, Smith; second-home, Spinks ; first-home, Walker. The match to-day is against Blackley Ist at Blackey.

div.head: HAMPSTEAD MURDER.
div.p: THE HAMPSTEAD MURDER.

MRS. PEARCY SENT FOR TRIAL. At the Marylebone Police Court, London, on Tuesday, Eleanor Wheeler, otherwise Mrs. Pearcy, was brought up before Mr. Cook on remand charged with the murder of Mrs. Phcebe Hogg and her infant daughter, on the 24th of October last*, at Kentish Town. The prisoner was very self-possessed, and her health had evidently not suffered through her imprisonment. Mr. C. F. Gill, instructed by Mr. Williamson, of the Treasury, pro- secuted ; Mr. Grain appeared for Mr. Hogg, and Mr. Preke Palmer for the prisoner. Detective Edward Parsons was called, and gave testi- mony as to the examination of bloodstains in the I kitchen. He was for a time in the front room with the prisoner at 2, Priory-road. She said: "I have not told a lie. I have not been asked a question. Mrs. Hogg did come here at six o'clock, and asked me to lend her 2s. and mind the child. I told her I could not lend her the money as I had none, and I could not mind the child as I I was going out. I told Clara Hogg about it, and she advised me to say nothing about it. as it would be such a disgrace if people thought her husband kept her short of money." Afterwards the prisoner said, "I do not enjoy very good health. On the Thursday night when I came kome my nose bled violently." Dr. Bond, of Westminster Hospital, said that on the day following the post-mortem examination he was shown a poker at 2, Priory-st. He formed an opinion that it was a likely weapon to have caused the wounds which he found on the head. There was one fracture of the skull which corresponded pretty accurately with the bow or handle of the poker. He examined the wound on the throat very closely, and the cuts must have been made with a sharpe instrument. He examined the kitchen at 2. Piory-st. He noticed that two of the lower panes of glass in the window were broken, and that the glass had fallen out into the yard. There were splashes of blood on every pane of the window, .but more on the broken ones. The spots were not like those resulting from the spurting of blood from an artery, as they would then be oval. They appeared to have been caused by blows from a heavy instrument. Some of the hairs found in the prisoner's kitchen corresponded with those of the deceased woman. On the 28th October he saw the prisoner at Camden Town Police Station and examined her hands. The right hand had scratches on the second and third lingers about half an inch long, and on the third finger an abrasion of the skin. On the left hand there were three abrasions on the back of the thumb and on the little finger. On the right hand there was a scratch and an abrasion. These wounds were all comparatively recent, and might hays been inflicted within a day or two. They were not such cuts as he would expect a knife to make—possibly some might have been done by finger nails. He did not notice any swelling of the prisoner's hands or scratches on her wrist. He did not further examine the pri- soner. He had examined the bassinette which had been found. It was stained a great deal on the inside with blood. There were rents in the lining, and there were hairs in it which corresponded with those of the prisoner. The Magistrate: In colour? Mr. Bond: Yes, and under microscopic examina- tion. The prisoner said she would reserve her defence, and was committed for trial on both charges.

div.head: TILE RECENT CHESHIRE POLICE INQUIRY.'
div.p: TILE RECENT CHESHIRE POLICE INQUIRY.'

At a special meeting of the Standing Joint Com- mittee of Ckeshire, held at Chester Castle on Satur- day, convened mainly for the purpose of discussing the report (already published) of tbe sub-committee Of inquiry into Mr. Slater Lewis's charge against , the Cheshire police, Colonel C. H. France-Hayhurst was unanimously re-elected chairman for the ensu- ing.year. With reference to the more important 'business of the meeting, Dr. Hodgson (Crewe) moved the following resolution That the report of the sub-committee of inquiry into the allegations against the police be approved and adopted." (Hear, hear.) Ho thought they should all agree as to the general value of the report as a whole. Quite pro- bably they might differ as to some of the detailed references which occurred in the report: but he thought that, in the main, they should all agree that the report was a vety fair one. (Heal, hear.) He wanted, however, to make some little detailed analysis of the charges referred to in the report; but he hoped that the end of the discussion would be that there would be no friction left anywhere. (Hear, bear.) With reference to the first gemeral accusa- tion, that of irregularities amongst the police at Run- corn from 1888 to 1889," much in excess of an ordinary proportion of such irregularities," Dr. Hodgson said that,including Superintendent Hollingworth, seven out of 15 police at Runcorn had, during the period named, been reported for drunkenness. That was a lamentably high, an unduly high proportion, and whether it was in excess of the proportion in other places or not, it was a serious state of things. The personal charge against Superintendent Hollingworth had been fully made out. Coming to that part of the reportdealing with game and poachers, Dr. Hodgson strongly condemned the entry of poachers in the police journals as "suspicions charac- ters. He believed in calling a spade a spade, and that there was something radically wrong in this practice of keeping a proper entry out of the journals and substitut- ing a phrase that might indicate any other class of offender. Such a practice tended to make the police crooked instead of straight. The responsi- bility for this, however, rested with the Govern- ment Inspector and not with the chief constable. He commended the committee's finding with reference to the game fund at Macclesfield. It could not be too strongly denounced that a minister of the gospel of peace did act as treasurer of a fund of this kind, the object of which was to assist in the conviction of men and the placing of temptation in the way of con- stables to procure convictions. It was too much temp- tation to place in the way of any man, and he was very glad that fund had been stopped and abolished, and he hoped it would never be resuscitated either at Maccles- field or anywhere else in any form. He was sorry that the chaplain of their county asylum at Macclesfield had been the treasurer of such an abominable fund. Speak- inc generally, on the result of the Inquiry, Dr. Hodgson said the whole administration of the county police was faulty as compared with the management of a borough force. He endorsed the eulogium passed by the sub- committee on the chief constable; he believed Colonel Hamersley had discharged the duties devolving upon him to the very best of his ability, and that every credit was due to him for the manner in which he had discharged those duties. (Hear, hear.) What ha had to say was that no one man, whoever he was, could be placed in such a position so as to give satisfaction all round to the public and police. It was a bad system, and the sooner it was altered and made the same as that existing in boroughs the better it would be for everybody. Every policeman ought to have the right to appeal to a higher authority against an adverse decision by a superior officer. Coming to the cask of Inspector O'Donnell, Dr. Hodgson said he regarded that officer with somewhat mixed feelings, but he found that the exercise of discipline with regard to O'Donnell and Hollingwerth respectively had been very uneven. O'Donnell was placed in a position of considerable diffi- culty; he left the force with a good character, and if they could not give him anything in the way of super- annuation allowance, they might at least refund to him the amounts deducted from time to time out of his wages. Seine people said that the £.600 spent on this inquiry was money thrown away. He did not think so. (Hear, hear.) He thought they had had £6OO worth. (Hear, hear.) Mr. M. T. Graveson (Liscard) seconded the resolution, and said Mr. Slater Lewis was to be thanked for having brought forward this inquiry, because the inquiry had resulted in much good and the cost of it had been money well spent. There was no doubt that Inspector O'Donnell had suffered • his character was good; and not a single charge had been brought against his moral character. If any grant could be made to him, he (the speaker) should support it. He endorsed the opinion expressed by Colonel Hamersley. The fault was not in the individual, but in the autocratic power given to him. It was said that the Emperor of Russia was the most miserable man in Europe, and Colonel Hamerslev mist expect to bear his share of the inconveniences of such a position. (Laughter.)—Mr. Ralph Bates (Staly- bridge) adhered to his previously expressed opinion with regard to this inquiry, that the mountain had been in labour and had brought forth a mouse. (Hear, hear, ' and laughter.) He severely condemned Mr. Slater Lewis's recent utterances with regard to the committee , as grossly unfair. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Speakman (Run- corn) fully agreed with the resolution and approved of the report, but condemned the remarks recently made by Mr. Slater Lewis, especially with regard to the chair- man of thesub-committee (his Honour Sir Horatio Lloyd.) If there was any member of the Committee more than another of whom it might be said that he had conducted

the inquiry fairly and given Mr. Slater Lewis every fair play, it was Sir -Horatio Lloyd. (Hear, hear.)—The re- solution was then put and unanimously agreed to, and a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the members of the sub-committee.

div.head: TERRIBLE MURDER IN MADRID.
div.p: TERRIBLE MURDER IN MADRID.

The body of a woman cut into separate pieces was found on Monday morning, in Madrid, in the Rua Ferro- carrill. A murder of an exceptionally diabolic kind has undoubtedly been committed, but who the murderer was no one knows at present. The woman's name has not yet transpired. The human fragments were considerably decomposed, indicating that the crime must have been ' committed weeks,.perhaps months, ago.

div.head: PROSECUTION OF ALLEGED PRIZE FIGHTERS
div.p: PROSECUTION OF ALLEGED PRIZE FIGHTERS

The trial of Slavin and M'Auliffe, on a charge of break- ing the peace, by a prize fight at the Ormonde Club, was I resumed at Newington Sessions on Saturday. Mr. G. H. Vize, the referee, was further examined. He said that when M'Auliffe left the ring he walked upstairs unas- sisted. Witness never knew injury to be caused by , gloves such as the combatant used. The contest was carried out on the Pelican edition of the Queensberry I Rules. It was purely and simply a contest for points. The charge against Slavin and M'Auliffe was resumed at the London County Sessions on Monday, before Sir P. H. Edlin, Q.C. Mr. Poland, who prosecuted, replied to Sir C. Russell. Sir P. Edlin, summing up, said that the jury were not to regard the contest as illegal because there was a prize offered. At the conclusion of his Lord- ship's address, the jury retired, and after nearly two hours' deliberation, returned into court, and in answer to the Judge said they were not agreed nor were they likely to agree. The jury disagreed, and were dis- charged, defendants being bound over in £5OO each and two sureties of £250 to appear at the next sessions.

div.head: TAUNTON RAILWAY DISASTER.
div.p: THE TAUNTON RAILWAY DISASTER.

COMMITTAL OF THE SIGNALMAN RICE. On Saturday morning, George Rice, signalman, aged 63, was charged, before the Taunton divisional magis- trates, with causing the death of ten persons in the rail- way accident at Norton Fitzwarren, on November 11, by negligently signalling the line clear to the. Cape mail train when the up line was obstructed by a goods train. Mr. Paul appeared for the prisoner; Mr. Clifton, of Bristol, for Noble, the driver, and Lowe, the guard of the goods- train ; and Mr. Bowen, of Paddington, for the Great Western Railway Company.—Frederick James Tovey, telegraph clerk in the employ of the company at Exeter, proved apprising all stations on the line between Exeter and Taunton of the despatch of a special ocean passenger train on the night of the accident. It was timed to leave Exeter at 12.44. The message was acknowledged from Norton. It was also sent to the Victory Crossing, near Norton, on the Exeter side of Norton Station, and was acknowledged. Albert Allen, signalman at the Vic- tory Crossing, proved signalling the train as it passed his crossing about one o'clock.—Afterffurther evidence, Rice was committed for trial at the assizes on the charge of manslaughter. The assizes open to-day (Saturday). Signalman Rice, is now seriously unwell, and has be- come deaf. Most of the injured are doing well.

div.p: THE OXFORD SHOOTING CASE.

At the Oxford Assizes, on Saturday, Catherine Theresa Riordan, 35, of Sidney-st., Fulham-road, London. was charged with attempting to murder Dr. Frank Bright, Master of University College, on the 13th inst. Mr. Reid, Q.C., M.P., and Mr. Lawrence prosecuted; and Mr. Darling, Q.C., M.P., and Mr. Turrell defended. The pri- soner pleaded not guilty. The statement made by the prisoner in the prison infirmary was read. In it she said that she fired at Dr. Bright to frighten him, and threw herself on the mercy of Dr. Bright, Mr. Dames and the Court.—The Court then adjourned for half an hour, after which his Lordship summed up, and said there could be no doubt that there had been relations between Haines and the prisoner that were improper and discreditable to both ; but they were those that were common enough,and on the engagement becoming known between Baines and one of Dr. Bnght's family there followed those outbreaks which were not unusual when such relationships were broken off. The jury must judge whether there was any justification for the conduct of the prisoner. The jury returned into court after half an hour's deliberation, and found the prisoner guilty of wounding with intent to do grevious bodily harm. The prisoner was sentenced to six years' penal servitude. The sentence was received with loud Noses.

WARRINGTON CRIUKET AND BOWLING
CLUB.

About 80 members of this CIO assembled on Saturday evening, on the occassion of the annual dinner at the Lion Hotel. Amongst the guests pre- sent were Messrs. E. Roper, C. Jones, and F. Jones, of the Sefton Club; Mr. Sutton (Birkenhead Park), and Mr. Rowley (Lancashire County). After dinner had been partaken of, and the loyal toasts duly honoured, Mr. John Fairclough, J.P., proposed " Prosperity to Warrington Cricket Club." Mr. J. Chidlaw responded. Councillor W. Pierpoint next proposed the "Health of the President." Mr. H. Fairclough, who received quite an ovation, said that when he joined the club, 25 years ago, he little thought be should oc- cupy the distinguished position as President. He congratulated the members on the position attained during the past year, and assured them that he should always take an interest in and contribute to the support of out-door athletic sports. (Applause.) Councillor R. T. Fairclough next proposed The health of the cricket, bowling, and lawn tennis captains," coupling with the toast the names of Mr. S. M. Crosfield, Mr. Thomas Morris, and Mr. E. White. Mr. S. M. Crosfield said that during the past year they had won ten matches and lost three. Mr. Thomas Morris and Mr. E. White also res- ponded. Mr. Harold Jolley, the captain of the second eleven, said that the second eleven had a good record for the past year, basing only lost one match, Mr. Walter Young then proposed "The Secretaries," and Mr. Charles Adamson, Mr. George Pilling, and Mr. W. S. Howard suitably responded. The President pro- posed the health of the Treasurer (Mr. W. H. Robinson), who, in responding, gave a satisfactory account of the finances, and stated that he believed, when the annual statement was made up in February, that the club would be free from debt. Mr. W. Milner proposed "The Isleighbouring Clubs," Mr. W. Sutton, of Birkenhead Park Club, responded. The musical part of the pro- gramme was exceptionally good. Mr. R. H. Pearson con- tributed a violin solo; songs were rendered by Messrs. C. Price, E. Roper (Sefton Club), J. Dewhurst. W. H. J. Jenkins, J. Perry, with banjo accompaniment; R. T. Fairclough, W. H. Young, George Pilling, and James Unsworth. A recitation was also given by Mr. Sutton, (Birkenhead Park Club).
CIFURCH PARADE OF WARRINGTON

div.head: FRIENDLY SOCIETIES
div.p: FRIENDLY SOCIETIES

The Friendly Societies of Warrington took a "new departure" on Sunday in organising their first church parade, and the success which attended it will no doubt lead to an annual parade. All the preliminary arrangements had been made on behalf of the Societies by an executive committee consist- ing of the following members :—Bro. John Emson, Prov. C.S., 1.0.0. F., M.U. (president) ; Bro. Samuel Dunn, P.C.S., Ancient Order of Snepherds A.U. (vice- president) ; Bro. Thomas Roberts D.C.S., Warring- ton District, Society of Druids (secretary), and Bro. Llewellyn Davies, C.S. United Order of Foresters (treasurer). The gathering was fixed to take place at two o'clock in the afternoon in front of the Town Hall and from that point the procession started at half-past two so as to reach the Parish Church in good time for a special service to commence at three. At the time of form- ing the procession there was an assemblage of between 400 and 500 of the members of the following societies :- -Independent Order of Oddfellows : Mr. C. Horrobin, Pray. G.M. ; Mr. Gilbert Riley, Prov.D.G.M. ; Mr. John Emson, Prov. C.S. ; and Mr. Thomas Wadsworth, dis- trict treasures. Warrington District Society of Druids : Mr. Thomas Eden, G.M.; Mr. James Simcock, D.G.M. ; Mr. Thomas Roberts, D.S.; and Mr. William Barlow, district treasurer. Foresters: Mr. William Orrett, C.R.; Mr. Henry James, D.C.R. ; Mr. D. Clayton, trustee; and Mr. L. Davies, P.C.S. Shepherds: Mr. Samuel Dunn, P.C.S. • Mr. Kirkham, D.C.S. ; Mr. Abel H. Mather, Pro. COr. Sec.; and Mr. Allen, treasurer. Grand United Order of Oddfellows : Mr. Matthew Massey, G.M. ; Mr. William Oxley, D.G.M. ; Mr. Thomas Taylor, C.S. ; and Mr. John Powell, treasurer. National Inde- pendent Order of Oldfellows : Mr. Robert Rathmill, G.M. ; Mr. James Bramhall, D.G.M. •' Mr. Isaac .New- ton D.S. ; and Mr. Joseph John Hands, treasurer. Gardeners: Mr. James Erin, D.S. The procession was preceded through the streets by the Volunteer band. but there was no display of flags and banners, and regalia was only worn by the district officers. The societies did not walk in any consecutive order a member falling in at any part of th. 3 procession he thought fit. t the Parish Church there was a large congregation ,and special hymns were sung. The prayers were read by the Rev. E. J. Wilcocks, and the Rector (the Rev. F. W. Willis) preached from the text, "Behold bow good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell ' together in unity." In the course of his remarks he said that ever since it was arranged, a few weeks ago, that a service should be held that afternoon,he had done his ut- most to provide a competent preacher, feeling the great importance of the occasion, and believing that good re- sults might follow. But, as they were aware, he had failed, and he had, therefore, been compelled to preach himself. It was while walking through the town the other day that he met a friend of theirs and of his who sug- gested he should preach from the text which he had just read. He considered the matter, and came to the con- clusion that lie could not have found a more appropriate passage. Having impressed upon the congregation the fact of their common brotherhood, he said they ought to feel the deepest love for one another. They had all been Proud of the great African traveller,Mr. Stanley,and they had read with surprise the description of the great dangers he bad gone through and had admired the courage he had shown. But what a thrill of horror had gone through the bosom of each one of them during the past few days as they had read of certain proceedings in Central Africa. They wished to make every excuse that could be made for the conduct of those in the rear- guard, but had not a shadow passed over the name of "Englishman" in consequence of the treatment of human beings, savages though they might be, but brothers and sisters in Jesus Christ? He was surprised that English- men could treat savages in such a manner. The Rector, in emphasizing the second point of his discourse, the unity proved by the Psalmist, observed that they had assembled that afternoon for mutual interest and to help one another. Very close should be the unity of such societies as those which had assembled in the church that after- noon. It was difficult in some matters for the English, Irish, Scotch, and Welsh to agree, but their boast was that they were one nation. Britain ruled the seas, and he urged them to discountenance everything which had a tendency to divide, separate, and break up. Their strength lay in unity. What was the object øf these friendly societies? It was to promote thrift, to make people more economical and not to waste their money, so that they might help each other in case of need. That was the value of their unity, which, he trusted, would never be broken. Other hymns sung, were and a collection was made, amounting to 12s. 4d. After the service the procession was re-formed and proceeded to the Town Hall, where Mr. Eden, who spoke from the top of the steps, proposed a vote of thanks to the Rector for his sermon. The motion was seconded by Mr. Dunn, and carried. Mr. Emson thanked the members for their attendance, and asked them to decide by a show of hands whether they were in favour of an annual church parade. The show of hands was unanimously in favour of the parade, which will be held next year probably in June or July. A vote of thanks having been accorded to the committee, the proceedings terminated.

div.head: TIPPERARY SENTENCES.
div.p: TIPPERARY SENTENCES.

Judgment was given on Wednesday in the Tipperary conspiracy trials, Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien being each sentenced to six months' imprisonment, without hard labour. Messrs. Patrick O'Brien, M.P., and John Cul- linane were also sentenced to six months' imprison- ment. Michael O'Brien Dalton, Patrick Mockler, and ThOlnaS Walsh were sentenced to four months' imprison- ment. The case against Father Humphreys and Mr. Sheehy, M.P., was dismissed without prejudice. Mr. Patrick O'Brien has placed the resignation of his seat in Mr. Parnell's hands, on the ground that Monaghan ought to be represented during the next six months. Four resident magistrates sitting at Tipperary on Thursday estreated the recognisances of Mr. John Dillon M.P., and Mr. William O'Brien, M.P. It was agreed to state a case on the power of the Court to estreat.

Whitley, the Bradford manufacturer who made a murderous attack on his wife in her bedroom, has been medically declared incapable of pleading, and has been removed to Menstone Asylum. While some men were cnirazed in a sewer at Man- chester on Tuesday an old conduit burst, sweeping away one of the number. Lieutenant Troup landed at Southampton on Thursday. The Queen, accompanied by Princess Beatrice, arrived at Windsor by special train on Thursday morning from Balmoral. The crew are supposed to have perished. The six men of the second battalion Grenadier Guards sent to prison last July, have been released by order of the Commander-in-Chief. A man named James Scanlon was killed by a boiler explosion on Monday in the engine works of Messrs. Palmer and Co., at Jarrow, two fellow-workmen being shockingly scalded. IMPORTANT TO CONSUMPTIVES. FUNERAL OF THE LATE MR- STANTON, OF THELWALL.

The remains of the late Mr. Henry Stanton, of Greenfield, Thelwall, were on Saturday afternoon consigned to their last resting place in the ckurch- yard of Thelwall. As no service could be held in the church, which is being renovated, the first part of the service was read in the house by the Rev. Canon Greenall. The procession was headed by Mr. Richard Dutton, of Lymm (agent to the late Mr. Stanton) and Mr. Rowse; and behind them walked a number of gentlemen (several carrying wreaths), among whom were Mr. Henry Stanton and the Rev, Wilfrid Stanton (sons of the deceased), Mr. Harri- son, of Snelson Hall, Derbyshire (brother-in-law), Mr. Bernard Stanton, Chorley (nephew), the Revs. Canon Greenall, Canon Guest, E. D. Garvin, and Hon. C. F. Cross; Major Fox, and Messrs. Charles White, Robert Davies, T. H. Lyon, Peter Stubs, Colin Maaver Harvey (Liverpool), Edward Greenall, jun., H. Greenall, Lister, Holding, William Houghton, and F. Taylor. Then came the coffin, upon which a number of choice wreaths had been placed, and it was carried upon the shoulders of a number of servants from Greenfield and villagers. There were also in the procession Mr. E. ilardisty (butler),Mr. Norman Taylor (gardener), Miss Griffiths, Miss White, and Mr. Bebbington (footman), and other servants; and Messrs. H. Roebuck, James Tuck, T. Fairhurst, Robert, Nathan, John, and James DitChfield ; William Darbyshire, William Wright, Joseph Wright,Peter Wasburton. William Ellison, Thos.Grounds, Thomas Speakman, Richard Shaw, and William Leigh. Then followed eight private carriages. The procession was met at the church gates by the Vicar of Thelwall. the Rev. T. Pyrn Williamson, who continued the burial service. In the churchyard we noticed the Revs. S. Wilkinson, E. C. E. Carleton, and F. Slater, and Messrs. J. IL Pickmere, S. Cbandlev, W.H.Bleckly, and William Owen. rhe body of the deceased gentleman lies in the family vault, on the east side of the church, in a coffin which had been made by Messrs. S. E. and H. Johnson, Bridge-st., Warrington,to whom the whole of the funeral arrangements had been entrusted. The coffin bore the simple inscription :—" Henry Stanton, born September 20, 1815 ; died November 12, 1800." The following is a list of those who had forwarded wreaths or crosses : Mrs. Stanton and family, the house servants: Mr. and Mrs. Jones Parry, the Rev. W. Robinson, Miss Lowry Mann, teachers Of National Schools, Thelwall, architects and masons engaged in the restoration of ThelwallChurch, Mr. and Mrs. J. C. Parr, Mr. and Mrs. Lyon, Mr. and Mrs. Peter Stubs, Mr. and Mrs. Edward Greene!, Miss F. E. Lloyd,Miss Jefferson,Miss Addison, Miss Bradshaw, the Rev. Canon Greenall, Mr. and Mrs. Shenton, Major- General Eaton, Miss Eaton, Mr. Ambrose, the agents and tenants of the estate,Mr. and Mrs. Charles Eaton (Abbots Grange), the Rev. Canon Guest, and the Rev. T. P. and Mrs. Williamson.

IN a shilling pamphlet of 133 pages, Mr. Reaney's published by Messrs. J. CLARKE "Apologia." and Co., London, the Rev. G. S. REANEY, at one time Ininister of Wycliffe Congre- gational Church,Warrington,endeavours to explain, to all who care to know,why he left Congregational- ism to become what he now describes himself to be, namely, "Assistant Curate, St. Mary's, Riverhead, Kent." NEWMAN'S " Apologia" is interesting, be- cause it lays bare the inmost psychological proces- ses,and makes it clear how,under the circumstances, be could not do other than go over to the Church of Rome. REANEY'S "Apologia" is interesting, but for a different reason. It is not for the revealings of the spirit that the book will be read, for there is very little of the spiritual element in it, but for the all-round hard-hitting at the pastors and masters he has left behind him. He admits that personally he has been well treated by the five or six congregations over which he has had charge; but he takes a cynical delight in exposing the weak points of the people he has been working amongst for so many years. It is tolerably clear from his own showing that Congregationalism has all along treated him better than he is now treating Congregationalism. The pamphlet is bitter where it should be mild—that is to say in its purely personal and semi-sarcastic allusions; and it is weak where it should be strong, for it utterly fails to reveal adequate motive for a most extraordinary change of front. After carefully perusing " Why I left Congregationalism," we are tempted to say of Mr. REANEY as BRYON said of Bishop BERKLEY—

Explaining metaphysics to the nation, I wish he would explain his explanation. Perhaps it is too much to expect Mr. REANEY to give an account of his conversion on consistent, coherent, and logical lines. It is not his way. He has from his youth upwards been prone to try fresh forms of faith—just as ladies take to changes in fashion. His first experience was of the Established Church, for his "father was organist of one ot the parish churches in the quaint and quiet little town of Huntingdon." "The religious people," he adds, "were mostly Dissenters"; and, whatever Mr. REANEY may now say, the same statement holds good to-day. For have we not heard again and again of the sinner,who, grown old and hardened, has explained his desertion of Little Bethel by saying he had "ceased to be religious and begun to go to Church." It is not, of course, to be suggested that Mr. REANEY in his descent from Dissent has reached this low level. He is one of those, rather, who are religious by instinct ; but ever ready to turn to "fresh woods and pastures new" in seeking for peace—and assuring themselves of pudding. He has not quite boxed the compass; but he has tried the Methodists, the Baptists and the Congregationalists, and he is back to the church of his early da,ys. As to his staying there, who can say? He refers to the influence which "a well-known dignitary of the Roman Catholic Church has had over him ;" and does not hesitate to say that—" There is much in Romanism that is true, strong and fascinating, especially as set forth in the works of Cardinal Newman, or as expounded by the living voice of Cardinal Manning." Just so; and when a man acknowledges the fascination of either a Church or a lady he is usually understood to be pretty far gone. But, fortunately, or unfortunately, there is a lady as well as a church to consider ; for a married man cannot become a Roman Catholic Priest. We trust to be forgiven for broaching such a delicate matter; but the "assistant curate "has been in some respects so frank in describing how he weighed " pros " and " cons " that we are inclined to think we should do him an injustice if we were to suggest that this feature of the case has never crossed his mind. Indeed, Mr. Reancy's pamphlet is a talk of shop, shop, shop, almost from beginning to end; and

what he brings out in distinct relief is that the Congregational shop is not as good a shop as he expected it to be, and that he thinks the Church shop will be very much to his liking. Perhaps, as to this, he may find himself mistaken; he has been mistaken before, and he naay be again. Mr. REANEY, it seems, becomes a Tory in be- coming a Churchman. He remarks, after a sneer at the possible tine "when Cabinet Councils will close with a benediction," that—" The leadership of the Liberal party is much more likely to fall into the hands of Mr. BEADLAUGH, the great agnostic,. than into the self-nominated control of a man who, is neither orator, statesman, nor scholar." And, in that extreme case, we should say all the better for- the Liberal party. But, as Mr. BRADLAUGII i 5! brought on the carpet, we cannot help wondering what Mr. REANEY thinks of "the great agnostic as one of the Parliamentary directors of the Church upon whose bosom he has just thrown himself. Does it fit in perfectly with his new notions of the • church's" historic continuity," and " her primitivo. scriptural teaching and practice ?" And, what if Mr. BRADLAUGII, as a future leader in the House of Commons, should succeed in adding to the articles of the Church something to his taste ! Would the man who has swallowed the thirty-nine Articles swallow a fortieth without as much as winking, one eye ? We should say not; for, by that time, the verdant Churchman will be a critical Church- man. He will have become tired of the huge fossil before which he, for the present, prostrates him- ' self ; and, sickening at the sight of ill-paid cural?ex dancing attendance on purse-proud prelates, he will have taken still another departure—fascinated maybe by General Booth, as commander-in-chief of the Salvation Army.

IT was MILTON who san.--" Peace Dr. Koch 's Discovery. hath her victories no less renowned than war " ; and the world is just now realising that the latest victory which Peace has won is likely to prove of stupendous benefit to the human race. The rush of medical men to Berlia during the past week is unexampled; and there has been something like excitement amongst a class ordinarily the coolest and quietest of men'. But they, more than others, percieve the import of Dr. Kocu's communications regarding the cure of tuberculosis; for they know that if, as is supposed, a cure has been found for consumption,science has won a victory the glorious results of which will be not for an age but for all time. There seems to be little doubt that the magic lympth which the G-er- man savant has discovered, or invented, is capable of arresting consumption in its early stage; and, if this be the case, it is a matter of course to say that, in the end, this fell disease will be driven from its stronghold in the human frame. The malady stands alone in this country as the most fatal that is known, for it is the dread cause, year by year, of one-seventh of the total number of deaths. It is the spectre which has, at one time or another, visited almost every family, and laid its icy hand on the best and fairest. Is it not natural, then, that amongst those who are quickest to know and keenest to feel, there should be a thrill of exultation at the prospect of arresting the ravages of this King of Terrors? Even now, whilst we write, consumptives from all European countries are flocking to Berlin with a view to being amongst the earliest to experience the bene- fit of Dr. Kocres remedy. Many of them are alas! beyond recovery; and one poor creature has died whilst on the way. It should be clearly understood, in order that no false expectations may arise, that it is not claimed for the lymph that it will, of a certainty, cure consumption in every stage. That is an issue to be determined by fur- ther experiments and close observation ; but it is regarded as established that it is a posi- tive cure for lupus and other outward tub- ercular diseases. A Vienna doctor, who wit- nessed the effect of the liquid upon a child suffering from "scrofulous glands of the neck," describes it as miraculous. A striking feature of the remedy is that it is so essentially a specific for tuberculosis that an unmistakably reaction follows its application wherever there is tuberculous tissue. In the case of lupus, this reaction ceases when a cure has been effected—that is to say when there is no living tubercle to act upon. It is the same with tuberculous lungs, with the difference that the lungs not being visible the final effects are a matter, as yet, of inference, rather than of abso- lute knowledge. It need hardly be said that the remedy is a very powerful one, and requires to be administered with special care. There is at least one instance in which a strong doee has been attended with fatal results. Some time must elapse before the lympth can be supplied in such quantities as to be general in its application; and Dr. Koon is fully justified in keeping the secret until he is assured, by cur- rent experiments under the eyes of the most eminent members of his own profession, that there is a trained band of physicians ready to apply the remedy under conditions which will be favourable to success. Dr. Komi has been experimenting for eight years, and the basis of his operations has been the tubercular bacillus the existence of which has been doubted in some quarters. His success opens to the imagination views of the possibility of attacking and destroying other bacteria which are, in all probability, the specific cause of the manifold ills which flesh is heir to. What a magnificent achievement it would be if we should be able also to attack cancer and fevers of all kinds, and kill them instead of letting them kill the patient L Life under such circumstances would be indeed worth living.
FOREIGN LOTTERY ADVERTISEMENTS.

At the St. Helens Town Hall, on Monday, before Alderman J. Harrison and Mr. W. L. Pilkington, Mr.. William Swarbrick, newspaper proprietor, was sum- moned on the information of Chief Constable Wood, for publishing a lottery called " The Grand Draw- ing of Prizes, guaranteed by the state of Hamburg." Mr. I. 0. Swift prosecuted, and stated the Act of Parliament under which the proceedings were taken. He went on to say that the defendant was the proprietor and publisher of the "St. Helens Chronicle and South-west Lancashire Advertiser," and for some time past an advertisement had appeared in that newspaper under a very taking and attractive heading. Mr. Swarwick expressed his regret that the advertisement should have appeared, and said he had no idea that the issue of the advertisement rendered him liable to a prosecution. Ho thought that ' as it was a foreign lottery there was no legal objection to its insertion as an advertisement, and would immedi- stelv discontinue its insertion.—Chief Constable Wood gave formal evidence in support of Mr. Swift's statement, and Mr. Massey, on behalf of the defendant, expressed regret that the advertisement had been inadvertently inserted. He agreed to discontinue all such advertise- ments in future, and would pay the costs of those pro- ceedings.—The bench, after a brief retirement, consented to the withdrawal of the case on the conditions men- tioned, but this would not be permitted in any future offences.

TOUCH AND GO:" The Queen ha l sent General Booth a sympathe- tic letter. She gives him credit for goodintentions ; but ho wants something besides credit—he would like to see a little of her Majesty's hard cash. ---•

Sarah Bernhardt makes use of a live snake in performing as "Cleopatra," and the reptile has, .proved so fascinating as to excite more interest' than the actress. Poor Sarah! But she is not the first woman who hairhad to play second to a snake,

Speaking it Grunsby, on Tuesday night, Lord Eisr tin gton said the Crimes Act had been "a bles- sing to the great majority of the Irish people." "A blessing in disguise" of course; and so much disguised that only Lord Hartington can recognise it.

The phylloxera has re-appeared among the most famous vineyards of France, and the price of cham- pagne is rising. This will afford a good opportunity for disposing of sham champagne. While the phylloxera is playing Old Gooseberry with the vines, now gooseberry is said to be looking up.

More of the infamous Crimes Act. Messrs., Dillon; and O'Brien are to go to prison for six months for inducing tenants to combine against their landlord—Mr. Smith Barry. No proceed- ings however are being taken against Mr. Smith- Barry for" inducing" landlords to combine. What is sauce for the goose is not sauce for the qanderl and that is the Tory Government's idea of justice

Dr. Vacher appears to have made bad worse by repudiating responsibility on what has come to be known as "The Hospital Scandal at Birkenhoaa." It has been shown that his agreement with the Corporation as Medics/ Officer of Health includes the charge and oversight of the Infectious Diseases Hospital. Ho has apologised for his mis-state- ment, but he has still a great deal to apologise for.

We must be thankful for small mercies. Mr. V. W. Legh, the member for the Newton Division, seems to be proud of the Irish Secretary because he has been spending a few days in Ireland. But little credit is really due to Mr. Ballour because 'he has at least done a part of his duty. He played :golf in Scotrand until—so great was the outcry against him—he was shamed into going to Ire- land.

There ic " confirmation strong as roroof from holy writ" that a number of the seamen of Her Majestis ship Serpent regardea the cruiser as a bad Baking vessel, and that they anticipated a •disaster. A feeling of this kind does not ariso withott, cause ; and the survivors should be ques- tioned on the point. No cruiser of the same build Ishould be allowed to go abroad until the inquiry is completed.

General Booth is to hare a chance of trying his scheme. He asked for 21.490P00 to enable him to make a start, and already about half that sum is promised him. There has been some sharp criti- cism on the supposition that-the funds would pass unconditionally into the General's hands; but he has cut the ground from under objectors by show- ing himself willing to work under a trust deed. This is as it should be; it will give more power to his elbow, because it will bring in more money.

-- The figures which Mr:-F. Monks submitted at the meeting of the Warrington Literary and Philo- sophical Society, as to expenditure in the United States upon educatien—and particularly on the Boston Free Library—were rather staggering to ' those who have only srist begun to realise that the local library is about to be made really free. They will wake up perhaps when they are made to understand what other countries are doing, and screw their courage up to voting some provision for technical instruction.

There has been a tremendous row in Dublin because Signer Foli, as one of the concert party which re ~ently visited Warrington, refased to respond to repeatedCernands for an encore. Are- call is undoubtedly 41 compliment; but it !must be for the artiste to attermine whether be will sing an extra song. The public cannot insist upon it as a right, and, as arvocalist's voice is everything to him, he is wise in refusing to strain it in order to "split the ears ,of the groundlinge Signor Foli had his way, and there was howling instead' of singing for the rya of the evening.

Some sympathy i•seems to have been excited at Oxford for thewoman Riordan, who was convicted of firing at Dr. Bright; for it is stated that the sentence of six year's' penal servitude was received with hisses. Dr. Bright was certainly not to blame for the conduct of his prospective son-in-i law, as to -whom thudge said "there could bens' doubt that Caere had been relations between him and the prisonerthat were improper and.discredit-. able to both:" The woman appears to have been terribly upset at the thought of being at aside, ; But it is the eld story—" Man to man soca •anjuirt is always so tis woman:"

Mr. Parnell is now amongst the mighty who are fallen. The wish was father to the thought that, as he had come out,cf the Pigott case with untar- nished reputation, he would clear himself of the charge wought against him by Captain O'Shea. But he has failed, and the taint will cling to him through life. IVe'shhil hear a good deal of his delinquency ; it is •it ssrt of morsel which will be' sweet to the Tory tooth—bitter as it isto the Irish Nationalists. Tlit•will in some slight degree injure the Horne Rule cause. But why should the peo- ple of Ireland have justice denied them because one man or a dozen men go wrong? Will some- body tell yes ?

The Railway Servants in the Warrington Dis- trict met in theLeaguellall, on Sunday, to sup- port the programme for shorter hours which is advocated by the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants. It ,is hard on them that they should work such long hoars as to need to meet on Sun- day; but there is no help for it. They certainly deserve every assistance and encouragement; for all they plead for at present is that their working day should be one 4f ten hours. That is longer than ordinary trades wdrk, and it is quite as long as is consistent with safety. The long hours worked at present air bad Ssr the men, and are a source of dar<ger tolit.e public.

It need surprise no one that Mr. W. Tinsley has , sent in his resignation as a member of the War- rington Town Council. lie has been treated ;shabbily, and he has hown a commendable spirit in resenting the treatment. His Conservative pfriends professed to befansions to do him deserved honour by maidug him an Alderman. They un- imously resolved on that •course at a caucas rneetingof the Council, but, because he could not ,see his way to travel Fr= the couth of England to, vote for hinzself, they just as,unanimously threw Kin over, and some of them voted for Councillor Askton ! Councißor Tinsley 's retirement is a dis- tinst loss to the Counoil—he is . cne of the better Aort of Conservative but what else could he do, andEpreserve his self-respect ?

ne Sub-Committee's Report, ariSing out of the ,Chesh:re Police Inquiry, was adopted at a meet- ing of the Joint Committee, on gatnrday. Most :people who have followed the proceedings will Agree at th the remarks of pr. ilodgso.l in moving rthe adoption of the report, which were to the effect -that drunkenness amongst the police of Runcorn had 'been lamentably high; and that, speaking gene- rally, the administration of county pelice was -faulty as compared with that ,of borough police. It is the syctem which is bad, and ought:to be re- -formed. It is to be hoped that .soraething will come of the suggestion to make a grant to ex- Inspector 'O'Donnell out at the Superannuation Fund. There has been no evidence that he neg- lected /p..s. duty through taking too much liquor.

Ells -in- ' LECTURE ON STANLIEY IN "DARILICT AFRICA:" juries included several fractured ribs, and death -en- ' On Tuesday a most interesting lecture on Stanley in sued a few hours later. Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy "Darkest Africa," was given in the Greenway-road by Mr. Moulton the head <master. The Board Schools, coroner, held an inquest on the body of the deceased at the Vine Inn, Thatto Heath, on Thursday. A lecture was profusely illustrated by means of the lime- ' got lantern, manipulated by Mr. Bowyer. 'The object verdict of "Accidental Death" was returned. I lof the entertainment, was to provide funds to continue the free entertainments to the scholars who :attend well during the forthcoming season. There was a large and appreciative audience, and Mr. Pritchard chairman of 1 the School Boardetir. Hewitt, and Dr. Gastaldisnembers of the Board were also present. The funds were con- siderably augmented by subscriptions from the members of the 'Board. The lecture opened with portraits of Mr. H. M. Stanley and the other officers who took part in the expedition for the relief of Emin Paska who was shut up in his Province in Central Africa. Having briefly stated the purpcse of the expedition,and pointed out the routo on the map, Mr. Moulton thee proceeded to give a full description of the journey. a was interest- ing to hear of the many difficulties and dangers encoun- tered in passing through the great forest wherecivilised man had never before trod—of the hardships endured through changes of climate and lack of provisions,—of the difficulty the travellers ead, to make the savage tribes understand that the expedition was a peaceable one,— and to know that through all this, the courage of Stanley never wavered, but that he pressed on, until he reached the goal he was seeking. The meeting with Emin Pasha, and the journey to Eastern coast, past Victoria Nyanza, and the mountains of the Moon, were afterwards des- cribed and illustrated. Before the audience separated, Mr. Howitt spoke a few words, and explained the object of the entertainment. ft is pleasing to note that the entertainment, both tnancially and in other respects Mese decided success,
ALLEGED LIFEBOAT SCANAL AT HOYLAKE A SCHOONER FROA RUNCORN LOST.

An inquest was held at the Dee Hotel, West Kirby, on Monday afternoon, on the body of a sea- man which had been cast up at Hilbre Island on Friday. The body was identified by Mr. W. M. Bhaw, seamen's missionary, Runcorn, as that of Captain Charles Curtis, of the schooner Blanche, of Plymouth, which left Runcorn for that port, with a cargo of salt, on thel7th ult., but lay windbound in the Sloyne until the 6th inst., when she left. He had heard of tine wreck of the vessel on the East Hoyle Bank, on Friday, the 7th inst., and the subsequent finding of the body, which he had no hesitation in stating was that of Captlin Curtis. A youth named Job Williams, assistant signalman at the Island, gave evidence as to finding the body on. the afternoon of Friday, the 7th inst. The witness was subjected to a severe cross-examination by the jury as to the efforts made by the Hoylake lifeboat to I rescue the crew of this vessel,but his explanation was not deemed satisfactory, and with the full concurrence of the coroner (Mr. Churton), the inquiry was adjourned for a I week, to have the evidence of the superintendent at the signal station, anylake ; also that of the captain of the lifeboat, and that of Mr. Jones of Hilbre Island. The remains of the deceased were interred at West Kirby Parish Church on Tuesday, and they was followed to the grave by the Rev. J. Pell, chaplain to the Mersey Missions,

, Mr. W. Shaw, missionary, Runcorn, and Mr. Marwood of Liver:vol. The rev. gentleman, conducted the burial service, and also delivered an earnest address in which he referred to ti:e work Captain Curtis had recently per- formed la conneeioa with a ten days mission at Run- corn. A number of dorsi tributes were placed on the grave.

Mr. Humphreys moved that the Board of 'Commissioners be recommended, from the end of the present financial year to grant the Library Committee the use of the library and rtading room premises ftee from the payment of rent." Mr. Humphreys said he had consulted the Law Clerk (Mr. Lake), and had ascer- tained that it was within the legal right of the Commis- missioners to grant the Library CoMmittee the boon which they asked. Out of something like £lB5 or £l9O, which was the amount of the library rate, only £4O to £45 was available in the course of twelve months for the purchase of new books, 1 newspapers, and bookbinding, while rent formed the by no means inconsiderable item of £36.—Mr. Grice said it would be a great advantage to the Committee if they had more purchasing power.—Mr. Hankiason said he should be glad to do anything lie could for the benefit of the Library which was doing a good thing for the town. —Dr. MacLennan seconded the maim' with pleasure.— In answer to questions the Librarian said the institution was pinched for want of funds.--The motion was carried , unanimously.—Mr. Humphreys said he had received several complaints from respectable persons of having t• wait an undue time for books —The Librarian said the complaint must come from those who had not patience to wait a reasonable time.—A discussionensued as to the practicability of opening the Library each evening in the week, and a sub-committee WIS appointed to consider and report on the best means of meetino•the demands for books.

ITHE PROPOSED ASSISTANT RELIEVING OFFICER FOR WIDNES.-Mr. Davies said that a month ago he brought before the guardians a motion asking them to appoint an 1 assistant to Mr. Treacey, the reliPving officer at Widnes. At that time the matter was deferred for a month, and he would move now that (subject to the approval of the Local Government Board), an assistant be appointed to Mr. Treacey, at a salary of £2B per annum. Mr. Tyrer said if they passed the motion they would have applica- tions from every relieving officer, and he would suggest that the matter be left over until the revision of the whole of the out relief cases were completed. After some digemmi2p, Mr. Tyrer's suggegtion was adopted by ten Votes to nia. This was the principal . usi bned. ---•
THE BISHOP OF CHESTER ON _THE 5111 P

7CANAL AND SCHOOL BOARDS. The Bishop of Chester held his visittttit to the rural deanery of Frodsham at Frodsham Parish Church, yesterday week. In the course of his re- marks he said there was no rural deanery in the diocese that was so largely affected as that by the Ship Canal; and great responsibility rested on the clergy. —The Rev. H. B. Blog,g (Frodsham) said the population in his parish had been considerably increased in conse- quence of the Ship Canal and all his services were a sue- cess.—The Vicar of Runcorn said he was very little affected by the Ship Canal labourers. The Vicar of Holy Trinity and the Incumbent of Weston Point could give more information than he could.—Dr. Preston (Holy Trinity) said he had little to do with Ship Canal labourers; Weston Point was more concerned.—The Rev. H. Wil- cocks (Weston Point) said they were a floating popula- tion. Sometimes his church was very full, and at others quite empty.—The Bishop said the Ship Canal Mission was not so distinctly Church of England as they might wish; but they had to be thankful that more had been given to the work ,in connection with the Church than they might have expected.—The Vicar of Frodsham said the drunkenness on the Ship Canal works was a hindrance to the work of the Church.—The Vicar of Christ Church (Latchford) said there was a great increase of drunken- ness in his parish, owing to the same reason ; but he got a deal of assistance from the offi- cials. —The Rev. Mr. Slater (St. James', Latchford) said a large number of the men hoed in his parish and their behaviour was extremely good. A great number of the children of navvies went to his school, and the school- master said they were the best children he had to deal with.—His Lordship addressing the Vicar of Appleton, said although hespoke as though he were not quite con- tent with the attendance of the parishioners at church he was glad to say he had a fair number of communi- cants. The Vicar replied that there were a large nnmber ot Wesleyans in his parish.—With regard to Halton, the Bishop said the report wag encouraging and the Rev. G. D. Wray said the township was the stronghold of Wesley- anlsm. His Lordship said Queen Anne's Bounty had seen put right and he thought the clergy would experi- ence a benefit. He was sorry to see that in three or four parishes Board schools, had slipped in unawares. Lie regarded them as a disadvantage, and standing in the way of the interests of the children and :;Rrents.— The Vicar of Heist); said they had not much to fat oi a School Board being formed in his parish. Ilislordship spoke in favour of the Church Army and district nurses; and alluded in high terms of praise to the good work accomplished at Ransom by Canon Wood.

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &c.
BY AN "OCCASIONAL COBILICSPONDENT."

That the Bishop of Chester's remarks at his visita- tion to Frodsham Rural Deanery, is highly inte- resting and amusing reading, and the Wesloyan friends will be glad to learn that in several of the parishes Methodism Is a power whose influence is felt even in the Churches.

That his Lordship appears to have a pious horror a School Boards, because the 3 were "a most lamen- table curtailment of the beautiful powers of pas- toral influence, and stood in the way of the in- terests of the children and parents." That his Lordship was speaking as a Churchman to Churchmen, and it is a fair surmise that his Lord- ship was not so much concerned as to the welfare of , the parents and childten its be was of the curtail- ment of the power and influence of the Church. That the Vicar of lielsby said there was not much fear of a School Board being formed in that town- ship ; but there W 4.1 s dir:useion at the meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, on Tuesday , last, which shows that a School Board for Ifelsby is not such a far off eventuality as the Vicar would have his Lordship nelieve. That the sanitary arrangements of the National Schools have been twice condemned by the medical officer for the Union, and he now reports that they constitute a nuisance dangerous to health), and he made certain recommendations which would entail the expenditure of a considerable sum of money if carried out. _ _

That it was said the vicar and school managers wished for a strong representation from the Authority so that it would be a " lever to squeeze the brass out" of the ratepayers as Mr. Mclntyre expressed it, and the Doctor showed the danger of the school authorities when he said they were in fear that a School Board would be imposed upon them, if they did not carry out the alterations. Mr. Brandreth said it was threatened that one would be applied for. That as a final to the discussion the Nuisance Inspector said,if the School Managers did not carry out the alterations,the Authority could do the work themselves, and, added the chairmain, "charge the ratepayers." That one can hardly believe that the ratepayers as ratepayers can be compelled by law to cotitribute towards the improvement and extension of a denominational school. _

That if the woik is done out of the public rates the ratepayers must have a share in the manage- ment of the school, but we are afraid that the vicar will have to fulfil the requirements of the Public Health Act and of the Education Code by means of voluntary subscriptions from his parishioners. That the ratepaye.rs of the locality are the best judges Whether thetr needs demand the formation of a School Board or not. That although no official doCumenta are presented' to the Board of Commissioners, nor any information vouchsafed to the public press,there is no doubt of a very large number of eases of typhoid fever in Run- corn, and that these are spread over every quarter of the town. • That it is said there are .50 persons suffering from the disease in Dukes Field district alone. That two patients have been removed to the hos- pital this week; but, for the little use this institu- tion is, under present arrangements, which are a blot on the administration of the Board, the expense of maintaining it might as well be spared to the ratepayers. That Mr. Dobson, who last year made an able chairman of the Health Committee, and took a deep and practical interest in the hospital, made a sug- gestion at the last meeting of the Board which de- serves earnest consideration. That he advocated that the hospital should be made free for ail, and there is no doubt the charges which are now made, are a great barrier to its use- fulness, and Mr. Dobson will earn the gratitude of those who wish to see the institution fulfil the pur- pose for which it was erected—to prevent the spread of infections disease—if he succeeds in carrying out the project he shadowed forth. That amongst the changes brought about by the construction of the Ship Canal, none will be more seriously felt and more sincerely regretted, than the extinction of the ship building works of Messrs. Brundrit of Runcorn. That the new waterway will absorb a portion of Messrs. Brundrit's yard in its course, and the Ship Canal Company require the remaining portion for other purposes, and the absorption of the works has thrown a considerable number of men out of em- ployment. That in the past the works have launched numerous vessels which are now trading to many qearters of the globe, and their craft always re- ceived the commendations of seafaring men for their general construction, good quality, awl adaptability for the purposes intended. That our local auctioneer, Mr. S. Yarwood, was -engaged on Monday afteroon in selling the valuable plant, &c., of the yard, upwards of 300 lots being disposed of under the hammer, and thus brought to an end one of the oldest industries of Runcorn.
