div.head: NATIONAL UNITED ORDER OF FREE
div.p: NATIONAL UNITED ORDER OF FREE
GARDENERS.

ANNUAL DINNER AT WARRINGTON. A most enjoyable evening was spent in the Old 1 Ball Inn, on Saturday evening, by the members of ' the Moss Rose Lodge, the occasion being the annuli dinner. There was a large muster of members pre- sent, amongst others being Brothers Councillors, 1 Henry Roberts, Beaman, and Flood (honorary mem- bers), Bro. James Budge (district master), Bro. James Hill (district secretary), and Bro. Davies (Lodge secretary). Bro. Venables (grandmaster elect of the order), was also present. A capital din- ner was served by the host, Bro. P. White, and, after the cloths had been removed, Bro. Councillor Roberts was voted to the chair, Bro. Councillor Beaman subsequently acting in this capacity. In submitting the toast of "The Queen and the Royal Family," the CHAIRMAN said it was nice for the members of the Moss Rose Lodge to meet together on occasions of that kind.to exchange expressions of good fellowship with one another, and to wish each other God speed in their walk through life. (Applause.) He was sure they all felt honoured by the fact that, their grandmaster elect was present, and they would all be pleased to hear from him words of wisdom and encouragement, words which would give them a stimulas to go on in the prosperous way they had done during the past twelve tmontlis and make them determine to work up their lodge so that it would nearly rival the lodge at Sandbach to which their worthy brother belonged. In proposing the toast of the Queen and the royal family he said he was sure the Queen had not among her subjects more royal men than the members of the Order ef Gardeners. (Applause.) *(Dhe CHAIRMAN next gave "The town and trade of NVerrington," and coupled with it Bro. Beaman. and in I doing so said Warrington was not the prettiest town under the globe, but for all that their homes were in or abont it, and many ot them loved it. They all desired tO see the town bright, and would like a little more green- ' ness about it ;but the latter was rather inconsistent, for they could not have vegetable life and commercial life at the-same time. But while they regretted that Warring- ton 'had ceased to be an agricultural place, they were I proud of the fact that the town had emerged from that bucolic condition into an active and commercial life, and they hoped it would go on prospering. Most of the industries of Warrington were in very healthy state, and they all heartily wished that this might long be the case. (Applause.) In response, Bro. BRAMAN referred to the amiableness of the chairman, and said be always aimed at the mark, and generally hit it. Warrington was& town that they all need-feel proud of, and it was a town of considerable importance two or three hundred years ago. At that remote period their Grammar School was in existence, and wien Liverpool did not exist, Warrington was a town of much import. The trades of Warrington, were •varied, and he thought they were all in a fairly flourish- condition. Most of them present were connected moreor less with iron, and let the corners say what they liked, there was nothing line iron. (Laughter.) He •remembered:a late Mayor saving that the iron workers °Warrington had helped to make this town, and he thought Wartingtonians should not take that as an insult. lier(the speaker) was also of opinion that men from Stallordshire oad iron workers from other places had also helped to make Warrington what it was to-day, and he hoped the present hopeful prospects of trade would con- tinue. That time last year they were looking forward to a splendid winter trade, but the push they ex- perienoed at the end of 1889 was checked, and they had a period of depression. But the future, to his mind, I was very premising, and he thought tht various trades the remainder of tkis year, and the beginning of next, would be iii a better condition than was the case this time last year. (Applause.) Replying to the toast of "The National United Order of Free Gardeners," given by the Chairman, Bro. Vast- entre said the United Order had just emerged from mister a cloud which had hung over it for a considerable time, and lie was pleased to say it was now prospering. Their number was increasing gradually, and they had in their secretary the right man in the right place ; and he was sure under his guidance the order would greatly extend. He sincerely hoped that the day was not far distant when they would see established a branch of tbe order in every town. He was pleased to inform them that they had a lodge in Belfast, and they had received applications to open others at Aintree, and Baxbadoes. A dispensation

P had also been sent for • the establishment of a lodge at Dernerhara, and from this they would see that they were spreading the order in all parts. (Hear, hear.) A mat— ter which demanded the serious consideration of all pre- . ' sent was the eteablishinent of juvenile societies. The• various societies who sent canvassers about insuring. children necessarily expended it geed deal of money it the payment of these men, but this money was saved is the juvenile branch of their order. TleT :nii,t remember that the youths of the country were the men a f the future, and he was sure they would meet with siteee,s if they initiated their children as members of a juve.:te !odge. He wished them every success as Gardeners, and if they ' would try, they could materially alter their position, and above all, he implored them not to let their membership dectease. To ensure this they must work only on one plan, ante this was the secret of their success. This secret was the speedy adoption of the graduated scale of pay- ment, and no lodge could live if it did not adopt this ISystem. In conclusion, he again wished the ledge every success, and heartily thanked the members for the en- thusiastic manner they had welcomed him, and drunk 1 hie health, (Applaule.) The toast of the evening " Success to the Moss ROSA Lodge" was next submitted by the chairman, who coupled with it the Secretary Bro. Davies, who, he said, was a capable secretary, energetic, and anxious for the welfare of that lodge. In reply, the Secretary said financially the lodge was in a healthy condition, although during the year they had had to meet several large items. He intimated that during the first nine months of this year the receipts amounted to £9O Os. 3d.,and the expenditure during the same period was £76 Bs. Od. The lodge had about 83 members. (Applause.) Bro. Taw then submitted "The honorary members and visitors," which was heartily received,and Bro. Councillor noon, replying, said in Warrington, they were in, what the people of Sandbach would call, a isongested district, where there was a great deal of rivalry surrounding them, for they had other societies to work against. They would fluctuate, as other orders did, Would rise and fall, and this they would be subjected to year after year. Let each member attend the meetings with a feeling that he was not doing so merely for him self, but with a feeling that he did so to confer good upon those who were unable to help themselves. (Ap- plause.) From the chair there was next given "The Press" with which was coupled Mr. G. R. Johnson, a representative of the " Examiner," who responded. __ .. . .. . _ . __

Following this the" Host and Hostess" was given,and this, which closed the toast list, was acknowledged in suitable terms by Bro. P. White. During the evening Bros. Prinsep and McKibbin enlivened the proceedings by singing several songs, and after "Auld Lang Syne" had been sung the company dispersed. The members, together with their wives and friends, assembled on Monday evening and partook of an excel- lent tea. The evening, after the tables had been cleared, was sent in singing and dancing, which was kept up until an advanced hour, all present thoroughly enjoying themselves.

div.head: ENGLISH NONCONFORIIITY.
div.p: ENGLISH NONCONFORIIITY.
LECTURE BY THE REV. J. GUINNESS ROGERS.

On Thursday evening a lecture was given in Wycliffe Hall, Warrington, by the Rev. J. Guinness Rogers, 8.A., of London, on What Nonconformity has done for England." Mr. Z. Armitage, J.P., pre- sided, and there was a very large attendance, in- cluding several local ministers. The CILLIRMAN said the duty of introducing Mr. Rogers to a Lancashire audience was a remarkably light one,. Mr. Rogers was a Lancashire man, and by all the asso- ciations of his early training and ministry, he belonged to them. They were thankful to him for coming amongst them on that occasion, to call attention to certain facts in the history of their Nonconformity, which some of their candid friends and critics seemed to think they had forgotten, or which the critics themselves entirely mis- understood. (Hear, hear.) There had been many events lately which made some of those dear friends. think that Nonconformity was going to the dog,and it had been thought expedient to take that opportunity of refer- ring to some of those events to which he had referred. and which would be the subject of Mr. Rogers' address. They wanted to address not only those within their bor- ders, but those also who were without, and those who took leave te criticise them so severely, and that oppor- tunity had been taken advantage of for the purpose. (Applause.) The Rev. J. G. ROGERS, who was received with loud applause, said he had come to speak to them simply on Congregationalism: what it had done, what it is dome, I and what it is capable of doing, for England, for English Christianity, for English liberty, and for English pro- gress. He observed—and he was very much surprised to and that the remark came from Lancashire—in the " Independent " newspaper two or three weeks atto an expression to the effect that Congregationalism was now felt to be on its trial. That, he confessed, rather startled him. He had thought that Congregationalism had been weighed in the balance over and over again and that it had been proved of full weight, true and sound, and he was somewhat surprised that a gentleman, professing to write as a friendly, correspondent of a Congregational newspaper, should deliberately say it was on its trial. In one sense it was en its trial. Since the day when Prince Albert said representative institutions in this country were on tlseir trial that had been a rather favour- ite expression. Well, if the "great mother of Parlia- ments,' as the great Lancashire orator once called the English Parliament, was on its trial, he supposed they must not be greatly surprised if they were told. that that church system, which he ventured to say- was the oldest of church systems—(applause)— was on its trial. He ventured, leiwever, to differ from the gentleman. He did not think that Congregational-. iltrl was on its trial; it was Congregationaliete who were on their trial, (Hear, hear.) Those principles which their fathers had handed down to them, and which in their hands produced great results were uot on their trial ;it was a question whether those who had suc- ceeded to the inheritance of those principles were worthy of them. Of one thing they might be sure. If their- churches grew weak the fault would lie not with thee principles, but it would lie with the men who had not strength and ability and robustness enough to work out those principles with efficiency and success. ( A npla use.): Congregationalism did not claim, never had claimed. and/ never would claim to be the one exclusive manifestation. of Christain truth, the one church in which alone Christ , dwelt, and beyond which there was no salvation. (Hear, ; hear.) They simply claimed that Congregational iem was.. one mode; they thought it the test mode, but they did not interfere with other men who conscientiously Wright, differently. They boldly asserted that Congregational ism had at all events vindicated its right to live, and had exerted an influence over the religious and political life of the nation for which the nation had every reason to be grateful. (Applause.) They did not even claim—and it was an important point which should be remembered in. the controversy that seemed to be suddenly springing, up—that Congregationalism should be the dominant church. (Hear, hear.) They objected to the interfer- ence of the State altogether, and they said, let every church develope its own idea of Christ's Kingdom with perfect freedom, and all they asked of the State was that it should give them space, and let them grow without. hindrance or check. That was whae they desired to see for all other churches, and that was what they asked for themselves. He was perfectly sure that in this age there was ne worse policy to encourage than the policy of attack upon other communities. The only class of people who coald benefit by those attacks were those who hated all their churches with an impartial hate. No true lover of Christ would ever desire to bring into disrepute the conduct and character of other Christian men, and the enemy of any one church was the enemy of all churches and the only injury lie was doing, beyond the injury he did himself, which would most certainly be considerable I would be the injury he did the Christian Church. (Hear I hear.) They bad no sectarian competition of that kid' in which they desired to take part. If faults eere im- puted to them they would do their best tei Correct and remedy them, but they certainly should not adopt the very unchristian and unbrotherly course which was very familiar in certain political circles. Two blacks did not make a, white, and he wa.s not going to hurl back any charge against the Established Church. (Hear, hear.) It had been said that during the last decade thirty-three ministers had left Nonconformity for the Church of England. That was not a very rapid rate of progress; it was only 3 3-10th in the year, and he would not say anything about the men who came over to them in the meantime. But he would point out, that converts, even illustrious and eminent converts, did not bring that acces- sion of power to the churches they adopted that either they themselves or their new friends anticipated. In stipeort of this he quoted some instances, one of these being the leaving of the Church of England by Cardinal Newman. The Church of England, he pointed out, did not suffer very severely through that defection, and there was the enost miserable contrast between the anticipations formed and the aetualresults. He need hardly say that the whole of the 33 would hardly match Cardinal New- man. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) As compared with him the whole of them would be but as the small dust in the balance. Mr. Rogers next referred to the good ser- vices readered by Congregationalists to the cause of religious and political liberty at great crises in English history, and he also alluded to the disabilities under which Nonconformists laboured until quite a recent period. The address throughout was a very eloquent one, and Mr. Rogers was loudly applauded on taking his seat. Councillor H. ROBEIZT3 in moving a vote of thanks to Mr. Rogers, said the spirit of the address they had lust listened to contrasted very pleasantly with the sentiments contained in what he might call a travers,ybyubotitftte aelnrn'e'ws Aslattod: logia" which some of them had just been reading. (Real" the gentleman hear.)h rr e was w hnoo twgrooitnegut;)a trpe production, ui cot oann say that the spirit of the address they had heard that night was a fitting rebuke to the spirit of the words Gr that traversty. (Hear, hear, ele ev n th?hkes Chair.whih antetdhonfP applause.) of so to waTsh he Rev. J. man brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
THRFT OF A

At the Warrington Police Court an Tuesday. Joseph Connor was charged with stealing a shirt from the shop of T. H. Poole, Sankey-st., on Monday. Mr. Hunt slid on Monday, shortly before three o'clock, the defend- ant went to the pawnshop of Messrs. Jackson, Winwick- st., and he there saw Peter Kelly, the manager, and pre- sented to him the shirt for pledge for 2s.—Kelly put the usual and necessary questions to prisoner as to whose the shirt was, and where he had got it from, and theprisoner said a man outside had given it to him. Constable Jones was then sent for; and, on examining the shirt, the officer found that it bore the name of Henry Poole. 'Prisoner was then taken in custody on suspicion, and subsequently he admitted taking the shirt. He was committed to prison for one month with hard labour.

div.head: SHOCKING ASSAULT.
div.p: SHOCKING ASSAULT.

.dit the Warrington Police Court, on Friday, Thomas Richardson, of Hardy-st., was charged with as- saulting his wife Catherine, on Saturday. Complainant stated that on the day in question, the defendant came home drunk. He used threatening language towards her, and refused to give her any money. He was a pensioner, and altogether he received £1 78. a week. Defendant had not given her money with which to carry on the house for many months. On Saturday he told her that if she did not leave the house he would knock her brains out. He then struck and kicked her. She was afraid of him, and he had threatened her several times previously. Defendant denied the assault, but the Bench thought an aggravated assault had been com- mitted, and granted a separation order. For the assault defendant was fined 20s. and costs, or in default one month's imprisonment ; and he was ordered to pay Is. 6d. a week towards the maintenance of his wife and child, and another child he was allowed to take.

div.head: DRINK THE CLONE OF THEFT.
div.p: DRINK THE CLONE OF THEFT.

An itinerant vendor of artificial flowers, named John Swift, was charged at the Warrington Police Court on Monday with stealing from the shop of Edward Smith, provision dealer, 12, Fennel-st., on Saturday afternoon, 4lbs. of bacon, value 2s. 81. The Chief Constable said that the prisoner stated he was formerly a clerk, at Liverpool, and had been there prior to Saturday. Shortly before 5 p.m., on this day defendant went into complainant's shop offering some artificial flowers for sale. Two or three persons were in the shop at the time, and, whilst Mr. Smith's back was turned defendant was seen by Mrs. Smith to take the bacon and walk out of the shop. She at once called her husband's attention to this, and he followed defendant and took the bacon from him. At that moment P.C. Phillips was passing the shop, and he took the prisoner into custody. When charged with the offence prisoner said "I've been foolish, but I have done it.' Defendant, who said he was inebriated at the time, and, consequently, was not accountable for his actions, was committed to prison for seven days with hard labour.

CIINNING THEFT. At the Warrington Police Court, on Wednesday, two labourers named Richard Lowe, of Gandy's-terrace, and Thomas Brown were charged with stealing a coat. value 7s. 6d., the property of John Gibbon, of Mersey-st., on Tuesday.—Mr. Hunt, in detailing the facts of the case, said about 8.30 a.m., on Tuesday,Lowe called at the shop in question and there sold Mrs. Gibbon a pair of long woollen stockings for 9d., and be then left. About nine o'clock Mrs. Gibbon had occasion to leave the shop to take a child to school. During her absence Lowe again entered and looked over some eld clothes that were on the counter. At this time a little girl was in the shop, and Lowe asked her if her mother was in. The girl answered in the nentive, and presently Lowe left the shop. As he was departing, however, Mrs. Gibbon was just returning but neither her or Lowe spoke. Shortly afterwards Mrs. Gibbon went to the back part of the premises to get a drink, and, when she returned she missed the coat (pro- duced). Both prisoners were ultimately arrested, and, in answer to the charge Lowe answered, "I have nothing to say," and Brown said "I pawned it for him, and gave him the monPy 3s. Ild. and the ticket.—Lowe was com- mitted to prison for a month with hard labour, and the other prisoner was discharged with a conviction recorded against him.

div.head: SHOCKING SERIES OP THEFTS,
div.p: A SHOCKING SERIES OP THEFTS,

On Tuesd;Y:37il;;W;r7ingt.i; Police-Court, Sarah Gavin, wife of Thomas Gavin, puddler, 12, Erwin-st., was charged with stealing from the back yard of Henry Ree.ny, 71, Dallam-lane, on the 12th inst., a dolly and tub, value 7s. 6d. ; also with stealing from William Kelly, 65, Foundry-street, a white singlet, value 2s. 6d., on the 16th inst., and further with stealing from the back yard of William Rowlands, 74, Dallam-street. on the 14th inst., a hearthrug,, value 10s.—The Chief Constable, in detailing the facts, said that there were four or five charges against the prisoner,but it was only necessary to take three. All the articles had been pledged, and, sus- picion being aroused, Detective Monaghan arrrested the prisoner. When taken into custody she said "Thank God I am innocent ;" but she subsequently admitted the whole of the thefts.—The prisoner said she had a good husband, and had no cause to take anything. It was all through drink and bad company.—Mr. Hunt: She has been dealt with for starving her children.—The Chair- man : It is an exceedingly bad case.—Mr. Hunt : She has a mania for drinking and pledging.—The Chairman said this was a very aggravating case, and it was evi- dent that defendant was not short of money. If defen- dant yielded to the evil influences of bad companionship and drink, he did not think she would reform. She would be sent to prison for two months with hard labour.
THE CASH OH PH/LIP O'BRIEN.

Considerable interest was manifested, at the Warring- ton Police Court, on Monday, in the adjourned hearing of the charge against Philip O'Brien. It will be remem- bered that defendant was brought up last week on a charge of drunkenness-and disorderly conduct in Naylor- st., on the 4th inst., when, on defendant persistently avowing his innocence, it was decided to adjourn the case in order that he, and also the police, could procure witnesses. Defendant, on Monday, however, brought , no one to corroborate his statements, and, after evidence 1 in reiteration of what was published last week had been given by Constable Clough, O'Brien was commencing to speak in a most voluble and excited manner, when Aldcr- man Harrison interposed, and requested him not to be so impetuous, but to conduct himself with propriety. Defendant's determination to speak, notwithstanding these magisterial strictures, appeared irrepressible ; and, in a stentorian voice he said sincerely, honestly, and truly he was not guilty of the charge. Last Monday Constable Clough went from house to house to trump up evidence against him. He wanted nothing but protection from the Bench, and he liked the police to do their duty in a straightforward, manly way; but the cowardly way in which that case had been got up he did not like.—Mr. Hunt said he had seen defendant at mid-day walking through the streets, and, without cause, had heard him use abusive language.—Defendant : I object to Mr. Hunt's reinarks.—The Mayor said defendant would be fined ss. and costs.

ALLEGED THEFT AT 131711TONWOOD.—A labourer named Thomas Mitshell. was charged with stealing three sovereigns from Peter Burke, of Burtonwood,between the 14th and 15th inst. Complainant said he was a farm' labourer at Bewsey Old Hall, Burtonwood. About five o'clock on the afternoon of the 14th inst., he saw prisoner in the farm yard. Witness agreed to proceed to War- rington with prisoner after they had partaken of supper. On their way to Warringtonthey called at a pullic-hour.a and witness paid for some drink. De.fendaut went back to the farm with witness and they both slept together overnight. When complainant counted his money on retiring he had three sovereigns in a purse, and he also had 9s. 6d. in silver, loose in his pocket. When he got up at six o'clock next morning he missed his purse. Witness commenced looking for it. and defendant asked him what he was seeking. Complainant answered that he was trying to find his purse and the three sovereigns, and said to prisoner that he thought he (prisoner) knew where the purse was. Nobody had slept in the building but themselves, and the purse must be about prisoner. He requested prisoner to get out of bed while he (wit- ness) made a search. Afterwards he found the purse under the bed at the side where prisoner was lying, but 'it was empty. Subsequently information of the affair, was given to the police, and the prisoner was taken into custody by P.C. Dugdale. In answer to the Chairman prisoner said he knew nothing about the money. He was committed to take his trial at the next Quarter Sessions. _ .

div.head: WILL OF THE LATE MR. DANIEL
div.p: THE WILL OF THE LATE MR. DANIEL
ADAMSON.

Papers tp lead to probate of the will of the late Mr. Mr. Daniel Adamson, of Didsbury and Dukinfield, who died- on the 13th of January, 1890, and whe was the first chairman of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, have been deposited in the Manchester Registry. There are two testamentary papers—a will dated 30th January, 1888, and a codicil made on the 26th of November' 1889. After giving leeracies of various amounts to certain of his servants and others, the testator gives and devices all his real estate, and the residue of his personal estate, to the trustees upon various trusts, which are mainly to allow his said wife to occupy the Towers, at Didsbury, and to use the furniture there as long as she shall think fit, and to pay to her an annuity of £2,500 year for her life. Tho gross value of the personal estate is sworn at £54,168 10s. 10d.

div.p: DEATH OF LADY ROSEBERY.

Secretaries of Football-Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warring:scu, not later ttan ten sealeek en Wednesday morning.

Lady Rosebery expired at six o'clock on Wednesday morning, at Dal menv. Lady Rosebery was the daughter and heiress of the late Baron Meyer de Rothschild, and was married in 1878. She leaves four children, two sons and two daughters. Her illness has extended just over a month, and began with a fever attack shortly after the family reached Dalmeny Park from London. The deceased Countess having been of the Hebrew faith, the body has been taken charge of by the members of the synagogue. Owing to her ladyship's death, Lord Roths- child's hounds will not hunt until further notice. The sad news cast quite a gloom over the proceedings at , Warwick when it became known, and much sympathy on all hands was expressed for the bereaved earl, and the orders to run Nuska in the Midland Counties Handi- cap were countermanded, and the mare sent home. _ _ _

_ Numerous telegrams and letters of condolence and sympathy have reached Lord Rosebery, the Queen and Prince of Wales being among the first to telegraph to his lordship their expression of sorrow. • Towards the close of the business at the Conference of Conservative Associations at St. George's Hall, on Thurs- day, Mr. Dixon-Hartland, M.P., said he had with regret to announce to the members of the conference the death of Lady Rosebery. They gave him all the sympathy they could, and were sorry for the great loss he had undeni- ably sustained. The good feeling of every member of the conference went forth to Lord Rosebery, and they wished publicly to express their great sorrow and sym- pathy with him in his affliction. Sir A. Rollit said in sorrow he seconded the expression of sympathy which had been expressed by the chairman. That was a mo- ment when they ceased to be partisans, and became sympathetic men and women. THATTO 11EATH T. RUNCORN RECREATION.—This West Lancashire Alliance match was played at Grange Park, St. Helens, on Saturday. Thatto Heath scored an easy victory, registering one goal, four tries and one minor, to Runcorn Recreation nil. WARIBNOTON RANGERS V. PEMBERTON SOUTH EN The return match of these clubs was played on Saturday, on the ground of the latter, and resulted in a victory for the visitors by 1 goal 5 minors to 1 try 'l minor. Cun- ningham dropped the goal for the Rangers. RUNCORN v. BUDITON.—At Burton. Withinfive minutes of starting Davies scored a drop goal for Runcorn,. and Abrahams obtained a try. After changing over, Burton. played a dashing game, and Ward dropped a goal. Result—Runcorn, 1 goal, 1 try, and 2 minors; Burton,. 3, goal and 4 minors. WARRINGTON Recs. v. ST. MARTS HARBIN RS,—This match was played on. the formers ground. Half-tinir, one try, six manors. Appleton secored the try, and Roberts made a good attempt at goal. Final result,. Recs. two tries, seven minors to nil. 'Tones scored the try. Andrew played well for the visitors. WARRINGTON Sr..ELPHIN'S V. LEIGH ERCREATION.— Played at Warrington. Leigh kicked off, the Saints-pres- sing at the onset, a minor resulting. Half-time arrived with no major point scored. Hampson restarted, and Warburton following up scored, the kick failing. The drop-out still found the Saints pressing, Bradley scoring, and again the place-kick failed. Final score—Saints. 2' tries, 5 minors ; Leigh, nil. Wroxes v. TYLDESLBY. —These old opponents met at Widnes, before a good attendance. Play opened very evenly,7and up to the interval nothing but minors were scored, the visitors leading by three to none. On turning round the play became fast and exciting,. Hanson at length crossing the Widnes line,, but the point was not converted. After some good play by the home lot Laws- got over near the post„but Brennan failed to convert,. and the game was brought to a close with the score— Tyldesley, 1 try and 4 minors ;.Widnes, 1 try. WARRINGTON" A" v. WIGAN " A."—The first match, of the season between these teams was played at Wigan, on Saturday, before a fair gathering of spectators. Tom Jolley, as captainof the visitors, lost the choice of ends, and commenced hostilities by a powerful kick. For the first few minutes the game was fairly even, until. Bandies broke splendidly away from a line out,, and passed to Rowe, who was floored underthe posts. Wigan, now got together, and a combined rush carried the leather to midfield, where the ball was passed out to Wallworth, who was pounced on by Jolley and the ad- vantage lost. The result of a pretty piece of passing by Randles, Russell, and Lally was- another fierce attack,. and several times Warrington were almost over, and once from a kick by Sampson, the home custodian, with bad judgment, tried to kick out, but the ball, luckily for Wigan, rolled touch-in-goal. Dropping out, Fair- dough got the ball away as far as the visitors' quarter,, but a grand rush, headed by Knowles,. Creaghan, neaux, and Barnes, completely nullified any advantage gained. A lot of scrimmaging on the centre line ensued,. until Sampson (who, throughout, played a splendid game) saved a rush in fine style at his own quarters,. a minor at length being conceded. After this, some fine. kicking was participated in by Jolley,. Sampson, and Wallwork, but ultimately Williams and Hackett got the leather to the Wigan posts. Here a splendid bit of cross passing between Williams, Rowe, and Jolley ended in the final pass being mulled, and the Wiganers got right away to their antagonists' 25. Randles, by some capital play in the line outs,. Philips and Knowles got the ball back again, and then Jolley, after getting spendidly clear, unwisely lost a try by pass- ing. Directly afterwards Knowles passed wide to Jolley, who forced another minor by a drop at goal, the half-time score being—Warrington a minors ; Wigan, 1 minor. Restarting, a mull almost let in the home team . during the first minute,. Sampson eventually punting well down the field, the position being further improved by Hackett. There was a tight five minutes near the Wigan line, Warrington once missing a rare chance, till Wallwork got the ball away. A couple of telling kicks _ _ _ by Massey followed, but i _ _

Wed grandly by a run and kick to the Wigan line. Lally was then pro- minent by a dodgy run, and the visitors lost a certain try by the ball coming in contact with the referee' a minor being conceded. The kick out was returned by Jolley, a rush by Barnes, Creaghan, Molvneaux and Russell carrying the oral further towards the Wigan line. Fairclough ran finely to midfield, Lally tackling him. Another capital run by Wallwork relieved Massey tackl- ing him finely at midfiel3. The game was finished in semi-darkness, the result being a draw—Warrington, 3 minors; Wigan, 1 minor. Throughout, the game was entirely in favour of Warrington, who missed innumer- able chances. Teams: Warrington : Sampson, back; Lally, Jolley, and Massey, three-quarter backs; Rowe and Williams, half backs; Creaghan, Molyneaux, Knowles, Barnes, Russell, Welsby, Phillips, Randles, and Hackett, forwards. Wigan : Atkinson, back ; Haddock, Wallwork, and Fairclough. three-quarter backs; Murray and Taylor, half backs ; Bithell, Grundy, Horsfield, Hampson, Prest, Seddon, Wells, Phearson, and another, forwards.
WARRINGTON T. WIGAN.

This match was witncssed on Saturday at Wild3rspool by a large crowd, it being estimated that .over 8,000 people were present. Nothing was wanting to make the match a success, charming weather, capital teams, and a• good game being forthcoming. Both sides were strongly represented, a hearty cheer greeting each team en entering the arena, and when they had taken their positions, they were found to be composed as follows : Warrington : J. Boscoe, back; H. Webster, T. Barnes, and J. W. Evans, three-quarters; James Bate and John Bate, half backs; H. Ashton (captain), Fair Turner, W. Nevins, J. Jolley, W. Berry, J. T. Thorniley, E. Dillon, J. Holmes, and T. Davies, forwards. Wigan: J. Halliwell, back; J. Slevin, R. Seddon, and J. Anderton, three-quar- ters; G. Wardle and J. Mitchinson, half backs; E. Bullough, J. Lowe, J. Walton, E. Dempsey, Darbyshire, R. Seddon, 3. Bibby, ITNamara, and J. Houghton, forwards. Referee, Mr. Seddon, Broughton Rangers.

Ashton losing the toss, Turner commenced on behalf of Warrington, kicking off towards the pavilion goal. Sed- don responded but feebly, Boscoe returning with advan- tage. After a slight stay at the Wigan quarter flag, Anderton came to the front, and after a spiriten run trans- ferred the game to the opposing quarters, but the inva- sion was staved off by Boscoe, who heeded not the approaching danger, and with commendable coolness made the Wiganers beat a hasty retreat. Holmes was first tin in a dribble which was the cause of .Halliwell subse- quently saving. This first point to Warrington was , the meana of causing them to play up with renewed [ energy, and another capital rush by Turner, Berry, I Dillon, and Ashton was luckily saved by Halliwell. Barnes essayed a shot at goal which was charged, and off-side play awarded Evans a free kick, play now being confined to half way. Free kicks frequently fell to the Warringtonians, but still neither side could claim any particular advantage, so evenlywere the teanas matched. Webster made a clever mark on the popular side, and , James Bate ran round the pack, but sure tackling pre- vented his travelling very far. Again Boscoe was , cheered for a brilliant piece of work, and Wigan again defended. A relief from the forward play which had become prevalent was noticed when the two Bates, Barnes' and Evans passed well, but Slevin was lucky enough to frustrate the movement, and Warrington quarters were invaded. John Bate charged a kick by Mitchinson, and although Jolley got clear, and Davies was prominent with a grand pi2ce of work opposite the grand stand, Wardle, by judicious kicking, pressed the Warringtonians. It was left to Webster to clear the danger, which he did admirably, and the movement be- ing ably taken up by Jolley, Turner, and Nevins, the game was taken direct to the Wigan line. Again the visitors cleared, and Evans passed across to Barnes, Anderton knocking the oval on. Warrington still at- tacked, and a beautiful spell of passing by the home half backs deserved a better fate. Webster made an effort from a pass by John Bate, being pulled up a few yards from the line. Barnes and Ander- ton each made their marks, but nothing Caine of them. Wigan now improved, and a forward rush by Bollough and Lowe was well met by Boscoe., A capital tackle of Slevin by Barnes was loudly cheered and then Bate passed high to Barnes, who failed to reach it. Anderton ran strongly here, and immediately after, as a result of a forward rush, Anderton struggled over, after apparently being well held in play. The point was allowed, and the scorer took the place with success. Wigan had a trifle the best of it until the call of half time, when the score read—Wigon, 1-0.0; Warrington, 0-0-1. On resuming, Berry met the kick off, and play was taken direct to the Wigan quarters, Jolley helping the movement with a strozg run. Wigan had an anxious time of it this half, and only on two occasions did they enter the home twenty-five. Barnes and Evans each put in tremendous kicks, and some passing be- tween James and John Bate, Barnes and Webster saw the latter having a shot at goal, the ball going a little wide. A palpably wrong decision by the referee spoiled a splen- did opportunity for Warrington, but, despite the misfor- tune, the Warringtonians still played with the hope that victory should yet be theirs. Amends were made for Webster's ill-luck with his shot at goal immediately after, for after the Warrington forwards had executed a com- bined rush to beyond the 25 flag, James Bate and John Bate passed across to Barnes, who out-witted Seddon and Anderton, and finally passed to Webster, who easily pushed Halliwell at one side, and a try was the result. This was a fitting conclusion to a brilliant effort, and Evans, who took the difficult place, failed to place the goal by a few inches. For the first time Wigan now in- vaded Warrington quarters, but the invasion was but a slight one, for a grand run by Barnes changed the scene. Slevin put in some long kicks to Boscoe, who was as safe as usual, and then 'Webster with a long punt took play on the verge of the Wigan line. Barnes effected another capital run, but, try as they would, the Warringtonians

Matches between Lancashire and Northumberland have always ended in such easy conquests for the-County Palatine and there was no variation to the rule on-Satur- day. Unfortunately Northumberland do not afford a trial on which much reliance can be placed, or we might look forward to the great battle of-the 29th with a- good deal of confidence. To win by three goals and half-a- dozen tries to a try should satisfy the most expeetant, but doesit not point to the very poorquality of Northum4 brian football ? Not much can be•said in praise cf the team that cannot prevent their line being crossed onmo fewer than nine occasions. To the oredit of Lancashire be it said that every one of the chosen fifteen was foand in his place,whilst there was only one alteration on the home side.

The magnificient passing of the Lancashire backs was- thefeaturs of the game. Nothing like it had ever been seen at Newcastle. The introduction at Berry has greatly strengthened this department, the Tyldiasley man playing splendid football, and being evidently able to pass the ball at any and all times. He gave, Valentine endless' opportunities, his unselfishness enabling the Swinton. three-quarter to score four tries himself. Flower and Gwynn were also of great service, the latter doing better than at Birkenhead a week ago. Coop was quite a sue- owe at full back, and he ought to be a certainty against Yorkehire. Tbe alterations in the forward ranks told a tale, though it must be confessed they were not very severely tried. Not many of the Northuvraberland'frfteenl showed exceptional ability, their antagonists being much too smart for them at every turn.

Yorkshire had not a great deal to spare in their fixture at Sunderland, on Saturday, as they °mid only beat Durham by a dropped goal and two tries to atry.. The score was a try each when the half-way house was reached, it was after this that the visitors manifested their greater skill, the goal being cleverly dropped by Dyson, who. was often conspicuous for his cool play and neat passing.' The Durham forwards played excellently, and behind Alderson and T. Crow were frequently cheered. Bonsor was missing on the Yorkshire side, his place among the half-backs being very moderately filled by Hartley, of Holbeck. Naylor was the smartest half on the field, and Lockwood was very prominent for his good judgment.

div.head: ASSOCIATION'.
div.p: ASSOCIATION'.

The Fbotball Association Council have thrown a new light upon the question of importing players from Scotland. /n future, if an English club brings over a Scotchman who had previously signed for another team and failed to get his transfer, even though he had not so much as crossed the Border, he will be rigidly• punished. West Bromwich Albion have now the pleasure of• keep- ing W. Groves idle for a month, that worthy having signed the registration form for Everton some months ago, and broken faith with them in the shabbiest man- ner possible. The Albion was astcnished to know,,that although,he had never played for the Liverpool olubi still his transfer was necessary.

Perhaps the best performance in connection with the League games of Saturday was the victory of Blackburn Rovers at Notts. The last named had not hitherto been defeated at home this.season. It was a very fine game from first to last, the Blackburn forwards playing espe- cially well. Bolton Wanderers had the satisfaction of beating North End at Pike's Lane, the Preston team again failing to score. The Wanderers had all• the best of the. play, Trainor saving repeatedly when the backs failed. Everton have again caught up with the Wolver- hampton Wanderers in the matter of points, and are really at the top of the League, as they have a better goal average. They could only beat Sunderland by a goal. It is announced that Jardine is leaving Bootle to join Everton, this new addition tcr their list of goal- keepers having been obtained at heavy nut.

Derby County seemed doom to stay permanently at the bottom of the League list. They were not in it with Burnley. Accrington failed to sustain their recent good form, and went down at Perry Barr. They are likely to remain in the last four, unless they improve in a very marked degree.

No English club appears to be able to master Notts Forest, who, in two days, ran clean away from Wolver- hampton Wanderers, and drew with West Bromwich Albion. The Forest may be heard of in the F.A. Cup competition.
MR. BALFOUR AND THE CONSERVATIVE ASSOCIA.TIONS:

The annual conference of the National Union of Con- servative Associations was commenced on Tuesday in St. Geerge's Hall, Liverpool. The Earl of Lathorn was elected president: In the evening there was a meeting in Hengler's Circus, over which Lord Lath= presided. Mr. Balfour was the principal speaker, and he pro- needed to deal with questions relating to Ireland. Mr. Balfour said that he had a firm conviction that some- thing more was required than the construction of public works or the expenditure of public money for the ameli- oration of the condition of the Irish people. They would have to change in a large measure the habits of a popu- lation, which, he believed, could be effected by kindly means, though not in rapid degrees. At the conference on Wednesday reeoultions were passed calling upon the Government to press forward the Tithes Bill and to re-introduce the Savings-Banks Bill. It was resolved thlalt no system of free or assisted education should be allowed to imperil the existence or impair the efficiency of the voluntary schools.. During the afternoon Mr. Balfour was presented with a number of congratu- latory addresses from Ulster. In the course of his I reply he said the Protestants of Ulster were not less acquainted with freedom than other inhabitants of the United Kingdom, and therefore he held that the charge ' made against him of being a tyrant was without founda- tion. Subsequently, the members of the Liverpool Work- ing-men's Conservative Association entertained the right hon. gentleman to dinner, and,. in replying to an address, he contended that the working-men of the kingdom were quite in accord with the policy of the Goverment. _ MR. RALFOUR AT SOUTHPORT.

Mr. Balfour, speaking at Southport, on Wednesday night, said he was getting bored with the task of track- ing calumnies and searching out the orlgin of every Separatist lie. Their opponents had evidently aban- doned the honoured paths of argument and taken re- fuge in hard swearing. He did not think it worthy of Mr. Gladstone to utter such amazing fictions as those he had uttered with regard to Irish land going out of cultivation, or about the reductions of Irish rents, or regarding the number of police in Ireland. Referring to Mr. Dillon and Mr. O'Brien, he said their play-acting in going secretly on board a yacht, and being pitched about for a week, was wholly unnecessary. They might, without interference, have gone on board an American liner at Queenstown. He argued that boycotting, even if not followed by violence, was destructive of the liberty of a civilised country, and declared that it should be put down by any means, even by shadowing.

div.head: LITERARY AND PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY. MR. F. MONK'S VISIT TO AMERICA.
div.p: LITERARY AND PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY. MR. F. MONK'S VISIT TO AMERICA.

The second meeting of the present session of the Warrington Literary and Philosophical Society was held on Tuesday evening, in the Museum Lecture Room, the president (Mr. P. Monks) in the chair.— The IloN. SECRETARY (Mr. J. Rymer Young), sub- mitted the names of the following candidates for membership :—Dr. Braids, Dr. Brooke, Messrs. Vere Davies, R. J. Chorley, and Scott Jones. No ballot being called for, the gentlemen were declared duly elected.—The PRESIDENT remarked that as he had never made claims to be considered a literary or scientific character, he had ventured to alter the sessional pro- gramme somewhat, and in place of "the President's opening address," had substituted a conversazione. (Hear, hear.) There were few opportunities in Warring- ton of meeting together on common ground in a social way, and he hoped, with the assistance of the members of the Field Club—a society of young men doing very useful work—to make the conversazione as agree- able and pleasant as possible. (Applause.)— Mr. Tnomes T. GREG, M.A., then read an inter- esting paper on "William Blake, artist aod poet." Mr. ROBERT DAVIES, after proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Greg, offered his congratulations to Mr. Monks upon his safe return from his long journey, and expressed a hope that he would, as a practical man, give them the results of his experiences in America. (Hear, hear.) They would all be delighted to listen to him before this session terminated or early during the ensuing session .—The Rev. F. K. FREESTON seconded, and the Rev. H. Giasox Szirriz supported the motion, which was heartily agreed to.— The PRESIDENT said that if it was the wish of the members of the Society he would endeavour to put his ideas with reference to his visit to America in form, if he could find time and could satisfy himself with the result. America was a country much beyond measure in material, moral and intellectual wealth. To show them the value which was set upon education, he should like to be permitted to state that when in the free library at Boston he made certain inquiries of the librarian as to its resources, and was astonished to find that the in- habitants liberally subscribed not less than £30,000 a year for the support of their free library. They also made an occasional gift of £20,000 for the purchase of books to keep up the supply, and, at the present moment, the authorities were busily engaged in erecting a magni- ficent building in which to hold the library, which would cost not less than half a million sterling. There were half- a-dozen technical schools for the training of 300 or 400 young students in matters appertaining to manufactures, minerals, and metals, and the authorities did not hesitate

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE..
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE..

Mk. Gladstone left Hawarden Cast% on Wednesday afternoon and paid a visit to his new and extensive library near the parish church. Mr. James Tomkinson, JP : (Liberal candidate for the Eddisbury Division a Cheshire)and Mrs. Tomkinson have been the guests of Mr. and Mrs,. Gladstone. Mr: Tomkinson accompanied the right hon..gentleman to the library. The sad intel- ligence of the death of Lady Resebery was received at the Castle early on Wednesday morning_ and Mr.. and Mrs. Gladstone, being acquainted, they were deeply .touched, and'great regret was expressed amongst the members of the family. Mr. Gladstone has decided to leave Havrarden for London on Monday next.

div.head: GENBRAL BOOTH'S SCHEME.
div.p: GENBRAL BOOTH'S SCHEME.

The•Eirl of Aberdeen has intimated to General Booth his•willingness to subscribe £1,001:0 on the conditions specified in M. Bancroft's proposal. It is stated that the demand for General Booth's book is unprecedented, two editions of 101000 and 40,000 respectively being ex- hausted, while.a-third edition of 50000 is being printed. Oh Monday night an enthusiastic meeting of the mem- bers of the Salvation Army and sympathizers took place at Exeter Hell' to hear from General Booth a statement of the present position of affairs in connection with the scheme propouoded in his recent book, General Booth t stated that over£3s,Boo had been .promised. The Queen,. acknowledging receipt of a copy of Gene- t ral'Booth'S book. "In Darkest England,!' says she has ' entire confidence in the author's wise and faithful stewardship of any fund that may be subscribed, and enclosesa cheque for £5O as her contribution to the good work.

div.head: ACTION FOR LIBEL AGAINST GENERAL BOOTH.. _
div.p: ACTION FOR LIBEL AGAINST GENERAL BOOTH.. _

In the Queen's Bench, on Thursday afternoon Mr. Justice A. L. Smith and a jury commenced the hearing of an action brought by Mr. William lames Baker, who carries-on business in Charles-st., St. John's Wood, as a marine store dealer,against General Booth, of the Salva- tion Army for libel: The plaintiff complained that the defendant had published a statement in a monthly perio- dical called " All.the World" whichimputed that he (Mr. Baker) kept a disorderly house. Evidence was called to show that the article was published without malice or gross negligence. The jury found for the plaintiff for AM beyond the 408. paid into court.

div.head: FINANCIAL, SITUATION.
div.p: THE FINANCIAL, SITUATION.

CONTINENTAL. AND AMERICAN UNEASINESS. The Central News is enabled, on the highest authority, to state that there is no foundation for the rumours current on the Continent and in America of the suspen- sion of the house of, Baring Brothers. The facts are simply that the house jamn liquidation of its acceptances already issued„ and amounting to about_ £15,000,000 sterling, backed by a.guaranree fund cuminethe who- amount. The Bank of England has undertaken to pay these acceptances as they mature. The state ,of the panic on the Stock Exchange on Wednesday was due to the fact that the Bank had declined to discount these acceptances in advance of their maturity. This, doubt- less, is causing great inconvenience to many holders, but it will be obvious that it involves no eventual loss to any except holders who are unable to await the proper maturing of the acceptances. The semi-panic in New York was due, according to the best authority, to the over-speculating in London, which has led many London holders of good American securites to throw them upon the American market,, where they were not wanted, and where„ by the volume of the offering, they have pro- duced a serious fall in prices. One of the ablest financial authorities in London, being asked on Wednesday what the result would probably be in regard to these American securities, replied" The people who are selling them to- day will buy them back again at 20 per cent, advance some months hence." The same authority stated that neither Amsterdam nor Berlin are selling Americans, and, generally speaking, the outflow of securities appears to be confined to London.

div.p: WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

the fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Alder- man Harrison presided, and there were also present the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Rev. E. C. E. Carleton; Messrs. Davies, Jolley, Hibbert, Gill, Dobson, Auk- landMather, Jn. Houghton, Humphries, Swinton, W Houghton,Kilshall, Dignum, Hood-Wright, and J. G. Sutton (clerk).
HPATINO ARRANGEMENTS.

The House Committee recommended that the kitchen boilbr at the Workhouse be repaired, and that tenders for carrying out the work of heating the tramp ward be ad- vertised for.—The recommendation was agreed to. ' _
THE SCHOOLS.

The Padget& Schools-Commi t tee reported that Mr. Evans who had been appointed assistant master had declined to accept the appointment, and it was therefore recom- mended that Mr. J. T. Bailey, who had else been an applicant, should now be appointed. The question of providino, a cricket ground for the children as recom- mended by the government inspector, was left over till the next meeting for discussion.—The minutes were adopted on the 'motion of the Rev. G. F. ROMIRTS seconded by Mr. ALIKLAND. SCHOOL FEES.
The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 54 cases 43 of which were old and 11 new cases.

TIIE WORKHOUSE CIIAP.LAINCY.—APPLICATIONS FOR A PLACE. The CHAIRMAN said he. had received the following letter from the Rev. S. Wilkinson, who was chaplain to the a 'Deoart S you are doubtless wm, olrk m Workhouse —t to‘ g Tifin'--Apersley as vicar. As the aWah:u place is only a sirrt distance f.rom Warrington, I shall be glad to retainovith your permission, the chaplaincy of the Workhouse, as it will be Possible for me to appoint a sub- stitute for the Sunday service." The Chairman said he had received another letter from the Rev. G. Allton,vicar of St. Darnabas., whih read as follows :—"Dear Sir,—As Mr. Wilkinson is leaving Warrington I beg to make appli- cation for the chaplaincy to the Union. The Workhouse • within the bounds of St. Barnabas parish, and it seems natural that the minister on the spot should have its spiritual oversight. Besides, at the time of my com- ing to Warrington Mr. Wilkinson held out as an induce- ment to me that the chaplaincy to the Union could be ! had. Under this impression I came and have ! waited for nearly seven years. Any emolument which could be added to this part of the town in the shape of funds, will be of the greatest use to me or my successor in helping to provide for the spiritual wants a this large, and rapidly increasing poor distriet. Thus I trust my application will meet with your favourable con- sideration." The Chairman added that Mr. Allton had waited upon him the other day, and related to him the inducement which, he said, had been held out to him, and he went on to say that Mr. Wilkinson said he would resign the chaplaincy in favour of Mr. Allton. Ile (the Chairman) told him that could not possibly have any bearing on the question, which was a matter purely for , the Guardians, and that it was not in the power of Mr. Wilkinson or anybody else to assign the office.—Mr. Ana- -1,,cc0 suggested that the matter better stand over until they saw who the new Vicar of St. Paul's was.—The CLERK pointed out that the two letters were quite distinct. Mr. Wilkinson, who was the chaplain, approached them courteously in that matter, and made a proposal which it was for the Board to deal with, entirely irrespective of what would be the result if a vacancy arose. The Board had first of all to consider whether they would be in favour of the arrangement. which Mr. Wilkinson suggested as to appointing a deputy.—The Rev. G. F. Rommrs asked if the Local Government Board would sanction any such arrangement.—The CLERK thought it would really be a question for that Board rather than the Local Government Board. Every person filling a public office mast of course be under such circumstances, both in regard to responsibility and other matters, as would best enable him to discharge the duties, and the Board could form a better opinion on that than the Local Govern- ment Board. If the Local Government Board did com- plain that it was not a c vrect arrangement they would do so when the Inspector visited the Workhouse. The CLERK also suggested that it was not advisable for any further discussion on the subject to be reported, and this suggestion was agreed to by the Board.—After some further discussion a resolution was passed to the effect that it was desirable that the chaplain should reside within the Union. The CHAIRMAN and others also re- ferred in complimentary terms to the manner in which the Rev. S. Wilkinson had discharged the duties of chap- lain.
This was all the business. ---.40.-

"A MEMBER OF THE WATCH COM- MITTEE" AND EX-P.S. SHAW. Sir,—The public having been regaled ad nausem • during the last few weeks with more or less garbled statements respecting the" cruel treatment of Ex- Sergeant Shaw," by the Watch Committee and Chief Constable combined, that even some members of the Town Council, who ought to have been better informed, have not hesitated to pour the vials of their wrath upon those two authorities ; and one gentleman with a courage worthy of the valiant " Bombastes Furioso," publicly announced that he had won his Election by making the conduct of the Watch Committee on this Shaw business alone the test question by which he defeated his opponent in the Whitecross Ward ; and further, this dauntless and irrepressible " Ajax " offered to fight anybody in any Ward of the Borough, and beat them too, on the same question, making it his " War Cry." Sic ! Now, as the public have not access to any official records of the facts as they really exist, I here pro- pose to place before your readers a few details for their information, and I hope guidance to a just and impartial view of this irritating subject. Constable Shaw joined the Force in 1831, and his conduct on the whole was so satisfactory, that on the recommendation of the much abused Chief Constable, he was ultimately promoted to the rank of Sergeant. Up to 1888, however, he had been absent on sick leave 144 days. On April 19th, 1888, it was discovered that he ,had been subsequently absent, at one spell for 103 days, ;and previously 35 days. The Chief Constable felt it his duty to drew the attention of the Watch Committee to tee constantly recurring and unsatisfactory absences, and said regretfully, he was afraid Shaw would never be fit for permanent duty, and that he should be advised to seek some other more suitable employment. It may be well to observe that this was two years ago, and that fact alone shows clearly that neither Mr. Hunt nor the Watch Committee were desirous of acting with undue precipitancy or harshness towards Sergeant Shaw. Let us now approach more recent dates and details. On May 13th of the present year, notwithstanding his frequent absences, he, Shaw, was granted by the "cruel "Watch Committee, on the recommendation of the no less " cruel " Chief Constable, a fortnight's holi- day, and when he returned he was apparently not well, and was again absent for 9 days. He resumed duty on the 19th June, only to be succeeded by a further absence of 34 days. In the meantime, viz., on the 27th May, the Chief Constable stated in his report to the Watch Com- mittee " 'filet in order to maintain the efficiency of the Force, a healthier and more active man than Sergeant Shaw should be employed, as it was manifestly unfair to the other Sergeants and Inspectors that they should be continually called upon to do his work in addition to their own, and for which he was being paid." The Chief Con- stable was accordingly instructed to apprize Shaw of the impending change in his position' but to which he, Shaw, made no reply ; and since then, he has been absent on sick leave for 21 days. At 9 a.m. on Tuesday July 24th last, the Chief Constable again considered it necessary to speak to Sergeant Shaw as to his excessive sick leave, and in the presence of Inspector Spinks did so, saying that in the afternoon he should ask the Watch Committee to give him a month's notice to look after another situa- tion or be reduced to a lower grade, when Sergeant Shaw replied, " I shall kick against that. I am consti- tutionally fit and strong enough for police duty, and I shall not, therefore, look out for another situation." I This, and other things were said by Sergeant Shaw in such a defiant and insubordinate tone as to be subver- sive of all proper discipline. The Watch Committee met on the 7th August, when they were informed that Shaw had been again on "sick leave," and that practically he was no longer of any real use as a sergeant, being appar- ently unable to do his work. The Committee, having carefully, anxiously, and with much sympathy, consi- dered his position in relation to the duties required of an efficient sergeant of police, passed most reluctantly, the following resolution That Sergeant Shaw be re- quested to resign within one week from that date, to take effect at the expiration of one month, and if he declined to do so then, he might be permitted, as an alternative course, to remain as a Ist class police officer at 295. per week, provided, the police surgeon be satisfied with the state of his health and general fitness for police duty,and if he was not so satisfied, then that Sergeant Shaw must resign his connection with the police force altogether." On the 14th August Shaw appeared before the Watch Committee, and on his handing a written document to the Chairman, that gentleman asked him if that was his resignation ? To which Shaw replied," Yes, I want to get out of this. lam unwell, and not fit to be here ;" to which the Chairman replied." Very well, you are at liberty." The following is a copy of a letter from the police sur- geon, dated 2nd August, 1890 :—" Gentlemen, in accord- ance with your request, I beg to inform you that Ser- geant Shaw has not yet quite recovered from his recent attack of illness, a little bronchial irritation still remain- ing, and in consequence, I do not feel competent to give a final and definite opinion as to Sergeant Shaw's state of health during the coming winter. It would be more satisfactory to see him and re-examine him a month hence." But as Sergeant Shaw had, in the meantime, as above stated, given in his resignation, the police sur- geon's further promised examination and report was unnecessary. I must now show the financial side of the question as it affected Sergeant Shaw, by which it will be seen that the longer he remained on the "tick list," the greater 'was the pecuniary advantage to him, for not only was he in receipt of his salary as a police sergeant, but also .of his sick pay from one or more Benefit Clubs, of which ale was a member, so that, to summarise the "cruel injustice" to which Sergeant Shaw has been subjected. by the Watch Committee, aided by the no less "cruel' Chief Constable, I may repeat that Shaw joined the force in 1881, and from that time to his resignation he had been off duty 331 days (exclusive of holidays), for which he was paid the sum of £52 us. 3d., that is to say for doing nothing, in addition to which he had not a penny to pay for doctor's bills, or for medicine. Now the total payment made by him to the Superan- nuation Fund was £l7 ss. 3d., leaving him a clear gain of £35 6s. The Watch Committee were quite disposed to have sanctioned a repayment of the, or a considerable portion of the £l7 ss. 3d. to Shaw, if the Chief Constable could have seen his way to recommend it. But this he could not do, without incurring a great responsibility, inasmuch as it would have been absolutely illegal to return any portion of the Superannuation money to a retiring officer unless disabled by sickness, accident or

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: age. But Shaw himself put the veto upon that, by tell- ing the thief Constable, when he was offered a slightly subordinate position, viz., that of a first rank constable, at 295. per week with Uglier and less responsible duties, and which he refused, on the grotnd that he was consti- tutionally fit and strong enough for police duty, in ccrroboration of which statement, he, almost immediate- ly after leaving the Police Force, sought and obtained, and is now actually engaged in an arduous and respon- sible situation under the Manchester Ship Cana/ Com- pany. How does this harmonise with the statement he made to the Watch Committee when tendering his resig- nation, that "he wanted to get out of it as he was un- well and not fit to be there"? Or with his continual absences from duty, as before particularised? Surely after this plain, unvarnishsd statement of recorded facts, no intelligent voters will again permit themselves to be blinded by the rhetorical quackery of any unscrupul- ous candidate for municipal honours, who may here- after have the temerity to make this "imbroglio "a " test question " against the Watch Committee and Chief Constable.

It perhaps may be as well to mention that Sergeant- i Shaw was a member of the Police Mutual Assurance Association into which company he had paid between £8 and £9 by virtue of which his widow would have been entitled to receive at his death between va and £Bo,and in the event of his surviving her (and still being in the force) he would have been entitled to receive between £29 and £3O, all of which prospective advant- ages he has sacrificed, as well as his contributions, by his own foolish act of resignation.—Yours obediently. A MEMBER OF THE WATCH COMMITTEE'.

THE CASE OF EX-POLICE SERGEANT SHAW. Sir,—ln looking over the columns of the Tory paper of Saturday last, I find there is a letter to the editor signed "A Tory Well-Wisher." Who his informant is I do not know; but he talks about facts as though he had been pretty well informed. Perhaps he can tell the public whether lam the only person belonging to the police force who has had the misfortune to be off duty sick, or whether there are not others who hold a position who have had longer bouts of sickness than I have. If he does not know, perhaps by making inquiries he can get a list of those who are not weather-proof any more than I was. If the "sick leave" of every member of the force was got, I do not think that I should be so very much in front of some. But I suppose that I was a good mark, and the target was a good one, so of course I was fired at. " Well-wisher " says my sickness threw more work on other superior officers. I should like him to explain how, and how many hours a day extra they had to work when I was off sick, because I am able to say that they had no more duty to do than they would have had if I had been working. Now "Tory Well-Wisher" seems to be studying the ratepayers' interests ; and I should advise him to find out how they are looked after by the police. There has never been anything said with respect to one of my sick- nesses (out of the fifteen times that he speaks about), being caused through sawing up firewood at the Sessions House when I should have been working my beat, and looking after the ratepayers' interests. The saw slipped and almost cut the end of my thumb off, and of course I could not very well be on duty with my arm in a sling. I never dented that I had had the "sick leave." but I do contend that I have been most cruelly treated. If it was for sickness, why was I not dealt with the same as other men who have left the force through sickness since I have been a member of it? For instance, there was P.C. Clynes. who, I believe, got about £5O ; then P.C. Hitchmough £2O, and P.C. Fern £lO, and I got ',the dirty kick out" with nothing. There is justice! But I say it was not the sickness at all. If " Well Wisher" knew as much as Ido about it,he would alter his tune. I had to he got rid of by fair means or otherwise, because I would not lie down and be trampled on. Now, if "Tory Well wisher" is studying the rate- payers' interests, let him make inquiries some Monday morning when he sees a policeman in uniform, and his badge on his arm, carrying a large basket to the office; and then on a Friday evening lugging the same basket away from the office: just ask what he is doing. I have not the slightest doubt but he will tell what lie has got ; and if "Well Wisher" thinks that is police duty, why, I will give it up. I wonder if anything happened on his beat, while he was encumbered with his load, how he would be fixed ; and whether the ratepayers pay them to be made " lobs " of, when they should be working a beat? I am very sorry to see that " Well-Wisher " has no better beam to pull at than putting a man down because he happens to be a Nonconformist or Wycliffite. I should have thought that he could have found some better grounds to work on than on a man's religion or politics. He will do well to wait until I have given him the chance to sea which way I veto, as I have not yet had to use my vote since I could give one, as, being a member of the police force, I have not been allowed to use my vote. I am not quite, at any rate, as changeable ?ome people I know and could mention, who are just as changeal-lei as a weathercock, and don't know what they are. I keep to the one religion, and don't change my cost quite so often as some. Now, I do hope " Well-Wisher' will look after the rate- payers' interests, and see that the police do police duty only, and also see on a Sunday how many policemen it takes to guard one place of worship that has avery high spire. Then go to the other places in the town where divine service is being held and wait there until he sees a man in blue come to look after it specially,and [am afraid he will want something to eat before he can get home for it. I can prove that on a Sunday at twelve o'clock there have been as many as four to look after the one which I have mentioned, whilst the others in the town get nothing but a passing glance. Bear in mind, Ido not blame the policemen, for of course they are bound to obey orders, and dare not go anywhere other than where they are told to go. But it is so in this world—some must have all and the rest must do without. Now Twill conclude my letter, and I hope when "Tory Well-wisher" writes to the paper again ho will have the manliness to sign his own name, for, if he does not, I shall come to the conclusion that someone el,e is making the bullets for him to fire. lam sure, that if they are hie own, he has no need to be ashamed' of signing himself, the same as I do.—l ath, sir, yours truly, Ex-Police Sergeant ROBERT SHAW.

105, Manchester-road, Nov. 19, 189 M THE TERRIBLE MISADVENTURE AT THE GOLBORNE GAS WORKS. Sir,—l have noticed the report of this sad case in which two lives have been lost through the ammonia vapours. It is on all fours with occurrences at our own Intercept- ing Dep<its where the men are frequently" gassed," and if there had not been assistance and remedies at hand, deaths would certainly have been the result. Such an event is, of course, to he guarded against as much as pessible, and I may say that in the plans for removing the nuisance from the Intercepting Depots which I have offered to the Corporation, I have guarded against it by making it unnecessary, by reason of my construction of the store tank, for men to enterthe tank, which would empty itself. Although I have offered my plans to the Corporation, they have not yet been accepted.—Yours faithfully, Warrington, 20th November, 189 a.

THE LATE FEAST AT RUNCORN.

Sir,—l looked very particularly in last Saturday's issue of the Examiner to see whether Mr. Marshall had given, as asked for by me, the names of the nine non- officials who had a carousal at the ratepayers expense, to the tune of Ts. each, on the day of the recent election of Commissioners, winding up, no doubt, with the slightly altered festive song "For they are jolly good ratepavers," &c., but I find he is silent. Let us there- fore lay him tenderly out, and " bury him silently at dead of night with his Marshall facts around him." The matter, however' will not end here, for I, as a ratepayer, intend to oppose the whole charge at the next audit. In 1 leaving this subject for the present, I thank yal very kindly, Mr_ Editor,, for the valuable space you have al— lowed myself and other correspondents to ventilate thizo matter.—Believe me, youre truly, THOMAS ARROWS. Mill-brow, Runcorn, Nov. /9th, 1890.
THE SPINNERS' DISPITIM AT COCKHEDGII MILLS.

Sir,—A letter respecting a recent strike of spinnors .at these mills appeared in your issue of last Saturday,signed by "W. Yates." Statements are made in that letter which convey an untrue impression, and in justico.to our- , selves and to the men now working for us, we Nape you well kindly allow our version of these unpleasant hel- -1 cidents to appear. "W. Yates" says "Our ?..,rievances were submitted to Messrs. Armitage and Rigny, and in consequence of their reply to this commualcation we were called upon by our Executive to give in our notices, Sm. We say that before the men sent in tlyait notices on 1 October 16th, no grievances were stated or submitted to us, either by the men or by any Association on their be- half, and consequently no reply could have been given by us to this communication. It was not until nine days later, when having sent the men an intimation that if they desired to say anything to us, or to retain their situ- ations, there was no time to be lost, three of the spinners came into the office, and we heard of what they had to ' complain. The' grievances" to which these men re- ferred are not matters which would interest news- paper readers, and do not relate to wages or the quality ' of the work. Suffice it to say that they declined to with- , draw their notices. We greatly regret that men who ' have worked for us so long, should cease to do so. We ' do not expect from them or others any conditions more ' onerous than prevail in all well managed mills.
'Hof VICASPNER, SATUR 9A Y. NOVEMBER 22. 18g0.

div.head: ALLEGED SWINDLE OF A BURTON-
div.p: ALLEGED SWINDLE OF A BURTON-
WOOD FARMER.

Yesterday, at the Chestez City Vallee Court, before the Mayor and other magistrates, William Smallev, alias Blom, of 24, Lever-st., Manchester, and John Bennett, address unknown, were charged.with defrauding William Carter, 20 years of age, Burtonwood, near Warrington, at Chester horse fair, on Thursday.—Mr. Brassey prose- cuted, and Mr. A. E. Caldecutt defended Bennett.—From Mr: Brassey's opening, it seemed that the two men had been arrested as part of a gang of five or seven men under a charge of conspiring to defraud Carter in horse transactions. The prosecutor said he bad been swindled out of £so.—The Bench remanded the case for a week, and admitted the prisoners to hail in their own sureties of £.50 each, and two sureties of £25 each.

div.head: FLOODING OF THE StIIP CANAL
div.p: THE FLOODING OF THE StIIP CANAL

In a portion of the canal near Latchford Station the greater part of the watar has been pumped out , during the week, but more in the Thelwall direc- tion not much progress is to be marked, although the water even here has sunk considerably. We mentioned last week that it was intended to throw a dam acrossthe canal at Morris Brook. to facilitate the work of pumping out the water, and this work has been begun this week, as well as the making of another dammear Stathatn brickyard. The damage is much less than was at first supposed, and the number of men thrown out of employment is not so great as was reported to be.. On Saturday a diver was engaged in searching for the body of the missing man, but he was unsuccessful, and as yet no trace of it has been found. As many of our readers may be aware, the cocoa rooms at MorriSbrook are closed every Sunday, but Mr. Manning, on. Sunday last, invited a number of men who were at work to the rooms and supplied them with re- freshments free of charge. His generosity was much I appreciated.
KILLED OY THE CANAL RAILWAY.

On Thursday Mr. Churton held an inquest at Elles- mere Port on the body of George Williams, who was killed on the Stiip Canal Railway. The deceased was going to his work at Ince, walking along the Ship Canal Railway, when Elliott,.the driver of the engine Locker, came along in the dark and went over the poor fellow, cutting him in two. It was proved that the whistle was biown, and that-the deceased was in drink. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned.

div.head: TERRIBLE MISADVENTURE AT GOLBORNE GAS WORKS.
div.p: THE TERRIBLE MISADVENTURE AT GOLBORNE GAS WORKS.
FUNERAL- OF 'THE VICTIMS.

Almost the sole topic-in Golborne since Friday has been the sad affair at the Gas Works. At the funeral of the victims on Saturday, there was a large con- course of sympathetic •ftiericls• and spectators. The burial took place in the parish churchyard, the Rector, the Rev. T. W:. Richardson, conducting the service. Mr. Glover being an ord officer in the Lan- cashire Hussars, his funeral was attended by several members of the troop to which he had belonged. Blinds were drawn and shutters closed while the cortege passed through the village. INQUE&E.

The adjourned inquiry into the circumstances attend- ing the deaths was held on Monday- afternoon at the Victoria Hotel, High-st. by Mr. 8- Brighouse, coroner for South West Lancashire. ltik. Jl.. E. Worslev, solici- tor, Warrington, attended on, behalf of the Gas Com- pany. Mr. Joshua Hincks. (Wavertree), father of the deceased gas manager, .was alk) present. Evidence as to the accident was given. by Jbhn B. Glover, son of Adam Glover. one of the victims;; Thomas Widdows, a stoker at the Gas Works ; :John, Walley, Patrick Dunn. Joseph Ashton, Dr. James Diblo, and P.C. Davenport.— Mr. Worsley put in an agreement made between Mr. Hincks and the Gas Company on his appointment, as manager, in December. 186 The Coroner read portions of the document, which stated'that one of the duties of the manager was to attend to the general repairs of the plant about the works.—The jiiry returned in both cases a verdict of "Accidental deattirempressing an opinion that both lives might have been savedif there had been ventilation and better access to the tank.—The.. Coroner complimented the jury on, whathetermed,their sensible verdict.

John Lowe and Sons, undertakers, Golborne.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION. TO TIIE BURGESSES OF ST. JOHN'S WARD. LAMES AND GENTLEMEN,—A vacancy having occurred in your Ward through the elevation of your late representative, Mr. John Platt, to the Aldermanic Bench, I have been solic- ited by a number of the electors to allow myself to be put in nomination for the vacant seat, and, having consented, I now offer myself for your sufferages. For seventeen years I have been engaged in business in the old North-East Ward of which St. John's Ward is a section, and therefore am no stranger amongst you. For several-years past I have taken an active interest in the many local questions that have agitated the public mina. The question of the Intercepting Depots is one which I know closely concerns the well-being and comfort of a great number of the electors, and, having ascertained the opinions of those who live in their immediate vicinity.find who should, therefore, be the best judges as to whether they constitute a grievance or not, I should be prepared to support the adoption of any remedy, however drastic, for their improve- ment, and, failing that, I should not hesitate to vote for their abolition. Attention as early as possible should be given by the Coml. ell to the unsatisfactory state of many of toe streets in the Ward, which in rainy weather, are in a deplorable condition. I am desirous of seeing, early in the coming year, the lend- ing department of our Library free, as is the case in some Of our neighbouring towns not near solpopulous as our own. Another question is that of the Public Malls, and I shall heartily support any scheme for their improvement, so that the greatest facilities and enccuragenaent may be given to all classes to use them, and particularly the young that they may under favourable conditions acquire the art of swimming. These, and many other questions affecting the economical and efficient government of the town, should you do me the honour to elect me as your representative, shall receive my most earnest attention.—l am, LadieCand Gentlemen, your obedient servant, FELIX LOUGHLIN. 17, Buttermarket-st., Warrington, Nov. 14. 1890.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION. ST. JOHN'S WARD. TO THE BURGESSES OF THH . WARD. LIMAS AND GIINTLIMUN.—At the request of a large and Influential body of the Ratepayers of the Ward, I have much pleasure in again offering myself as a candidate for election to fill the vacancy caused by Mr. Platt being appointed Alder- man. Should you do me the honour to elect me. my constant Object in the Council will be to do all in my power for the Improvement of the Town and its Trade, so as to create Labour and Wages for the Working Classes and Business for the Shopkeepers and Commercial Interest. My best attention will be given to the Improvement of your Streets, Workingmen's Houses, the supply of good Gas at as low a rate as possible, the Improvement of the Sanitary Arrangements of the Town. and to full efficiency with due economy in all matters connected with the Ward and Borough. As regards the Intercepting Depat so cruelly planted in your midst, I shall do all in my power to have it swept away and entirely removed. I RITI also strongly in favour a the nightsoil being removed during the night, and thus do away with the nuisance of having to meet bad smelling carts lathe streets at all hours of the day. I am a resident in your Ward, your interests and mine are identical, and I shall at all times be at hand and ready to hear the grievance of any Burgess, and. so far as It lies in my power, I shall endeavour to have such grievance remedied. Having lived amongst you for many years and being well known to a very large number of you. I feel that, I may with great confidence ask your votes and active support on the Polling Day, I am, Ladles and Gentlemen. Yours faithfully, JAMES HILL. 23, Blrlhall-street, November 14th, 1890.
